Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 1:

(p-232) In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Help is from Him, and may God bless the most fortunate of His creatures and the adornment of His servants, our master Muhammad, and his family and companions.

Surat al-Qasas (The Narratives)

Its central purpose (maqsud) is humility before God, which necessitates returning the whole matter to Him. This arises from faith in the Hereafter, and from faith in the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is established by the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an, and which reveals hidden matters through the tongue of one who never learned knowledge from anyone among creation, and which produces the exaltedness of the one characterised by it. This is what is drawn from its name "al-Qasas," in which Shu'ayb ruled, for the sake of which the exaltedness of the Interlocutor (al-Kalim, Musa) over the one who opposed him and the suppression of the one who was hostile to him, peace be upon them both, is decreed. So the outcome, in accordance with what He said, "In the name of God" (bismillah), who is singled out for greatness and majesty, clothes His servants with the garments of His awe; "the Most Compassionate" (al-Rahman), whose blessing of eloquence is general, even to the people of disbelief; "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who (p-233) singles out the people of faith with the blessing of what follows the resurrection.

When He concluded those (surahs) with the emphatic promise that He will show His signs so that they are recognised, and that He is not unaware of anything, as a threat to the wrongdoer and a steadfastness for the one who knows, and since the first of these (the threat) included what He inspires in this surah of miraculous methods from the hidden sciences of the People of the Book, so that they cannot refute it, and the second (steadfastness) included what He did to Pharaoh and his people, He began this (surah) with: "Ta, Sin, Mim" (Ta-Sin-Mim), indicating with the beautiful Ta, which signifies purity and goodness, the deliverance of the Children of Israel after their long trial which purified them, a great matter; and with the Sin, which alludes to loftiness, brilliance and sovereignty, that this will be through a heard revelation at the sacred valley (dhi Tuwa) of the ancient Mount Sinai; and with the Mim, which prepares for kingship and blessing, to a decree from the Most High King concerning all of that, complete and comprehensive.

Since these were lofty allusions, and what follows them comprises arrangements (nuzum) that contain the clearest of indications, He said, pointing to their greatness: ﴿Those﴾, that is, these lofty-ranked verses, ﴿are the verses of the Book﴾, that is, the one sent down upon your heart, which gathers all the worldly and otherwise benefits, ﴿clear﴾, that is, the decisive, revealing, elucidating, manifesting one, because it is from Us without any doubt, and it contains everything that is needed of that and other matters, for those who make it a matter of concern to them, receive it with acceptance, and give ear to it while being present in mind.

[p. 234]

Then he (al-Biqa'i) established the proof of its clarity (*ibanatihi*). And that He narrates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ, with what He included here in the story of Musa, peace be upon him, of the subtle details that few of their experts know, in a manner that informs about what He avenged with against Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and his people, and those who joined them, such as Qarun (Korah). He bestowed it upon Musa, peace be upon him, and his followers. For this reason, He expanded upon the matters of the story in it more than in any other place. So He said: ﴿We recite﴾, i.e., We narrate in continuous succession, one part following another, ﴿to you﴾ through the mediation of Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him.

Since the intent is only to narrate what is among the great reports as a clarification of the signs, with knowledge of the manifest and the hidden, and of accountability and recompense, and not all reports, He said: ﴿of the news of Musa and Fir'awn﴾, i.e., some of their great report, this news being connected and existing ﴿in truth﴾, i.e., that which the reality corresponds to. For We did not report in it anything future except that the existing matter at its occurrence corresponded to it. He drew attention to the fact that this clarification, as has preceded, benefits only those of submissive certainty, by His saying: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, i.e., who renew faith at every time and at every occurrence, for the steadfastness of their faith. Thus it is known that the purpose of it here is the argument for the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), the unlettered, through his awareness of the unseen, and the warning with His all-encompassing knowledge and His comprehensive power, and that whatever He wills comes to be, and there is no repelling of His decree, and caution does not avail against His destiny. Thus it is correct that it is a proof of His exalted saying at the end of that: ﴿He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them﴾ [al-Naml: 93] [the verse]. For this reason, the principal reports of the story were summarized, and the foundational matters of the hidden affairs and the subtle details of the deeds of those mentioned in it were mentioned, [p. 235] including Musa, peace be upon him, his mother, Fir'awn, and others, along with the wisdoms that you see, which none perceives except one who knows by learning or by revelation. It is known to every addressee that the first (learning) is negated for the one upon whom this Reminder was sent down (ﷺ), so the matter is restricted to the second. What clarifies this aim for you, along with this first verse I mentioned, is His exalted saying at the end of the story: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44], ﴿and you were not on the side of the Mount﴾ [al-Qasas: 46], and the following of the story with His exalted saying: ﴿And We have certainly caused the word to reach them, that they may remember﴾ [al-Qasas: 51]. So the intent of this context of it, as you see, is other than what preceded of its other contexts, as has passed, so there is no repetition in any of that. And Allah is the Guide.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When His glorified saying ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred﴾ [al-Naml: 91] to the end of the surah included intimidation, warning, admonition and threat, it entailed an indication that he, peace be upon him, would possess the city of Makkah, and that Allah would open it to him, and would humble the obstinate and rebellious chiefs of Quraysh, and would honor the followers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those whom Quraysh had oppressed among the believers. Then He, glorified, followed that with what He related to His Prophet of the purification of what He had alluded to from the story of the Children of Israel, the beginning of their trial with Fir'awn, his domination over them, and his killing of them, until [p. 236] Allah honored them and caused them to prevail over their enemy, and gave them their land and their homes. For this reason, the Exalted indicated in both stories: in the first with His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them﴾ [al-Naml: 93], and in the second with His saying: ﴿And We would show Fir'awn and Haman and their soldiers from them that which they feared﴾ [al-Qasas: 6]. Then He began narrating the affair of Fir'awn, his caution, his obstinacy in killing the male children, and then that did not avail him anything against the decree of Allah. In his condition there is a lesson for whoever is granted success in taking heed, and proof that He, glorified, is the sole Possessor of dominion, who gives dominion to whom He wills and removes it from whom He wills, and no restrainer restrains Him, and no preventer prevents Him from what He wills.

﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 26]. And the exalted saying: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession in the land﴾ [al-Nur: 55], the verse, has made clear what the summary of what we have clarified of its connection, from the end of al-Naml and the beginning of al-Qasas, indicated. We will add to its explanation by mentioning glimpses of the interpretation of what was intended to be connected. So we say: Indeed, His exalted saying, informing His Prophet (ﷺ) and commanding him: ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship﴾ [al-Naml: 91], up to His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ [al-Naml: 93], contains without any concealment a severe threat and stern warning. Then in His saying: ﴿the Lord of this city﴾ [al-Naml: 91] there is an indication that he, peace be upon him, will conquer it and possess it, because it is the city of his Lord and His dominion, and he is His servant and Messenger, and He has singled him out with His message, and everything belongs to Him. So servants and cities are His possession. Therefore in this there is an indication like that in His exalted saying: [p. 237] ﴿Indeed, He who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely return you to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas: 85], and His exalted saying: ﴿And that I should recite the Qur'an﴾ [al-Naml: 92], i.e., that they may hear it and thereby remember, and that whoever has been preceded by happiness may remember, and observe the custom of Allah concerning His servants and lands, and hear what befell those who opposed, transgressed, denied and were arrogant. How much more so when the story of [Allah] and His seizing (of Fir'awn), and his caution did not avail him, and He gave the inheritance of His weak servants' land and homes, and established them in the land, and honored His messengers and their followers. ﴿We recite to you from the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth, for a people who believe﴾, i.e., who affirm, take heed, reason, and seek clarity. His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ [al-Naml: 93] refers to what befell them on the day of Badr, and after that to the day of the Conquest of Makkah, and the submission of one who did not think he would submit, and the destruction of one whose rebellion and obstinacy had lasted long, and the submission of all the Arabs after the Conquest of Makkah and the entry of people into the religion in multitudes, and the honor of some peoples and the humiliation of others, in accordance with the rule: ﴿Indeed, the most honorable of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], until Allah opened for the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, what their Prophet (ﷺ) had promised them, and it occurred as he promised. When this verse included what had been alluded to, it was followed by what is tantamount to saying: Your arrogance is not greater than the arrogance of Fir'awn and his people, nor is the condition of the oppressed believers in Makkah, whom you intended to tempt in their religion, less than the condition of the Children of Israel when Fir'awn tested them by slaughtering their sons. Would that you had reflected upon the outcome of the two groups, and taken the clearest of the two paths.

﴿Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the outcome of those before them?﴾ [Ghafir: 82] [p. 238] up to His saying: ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾ [Ghafir: 82]. If you had reflected on that, you would have known that the good outcome belongs to righteousness. After the opening of the surah, He, glorified, said: Indeed Fir'awn exalted himself in the land, then He mentioned from his story what contains a lesson, and He mentioned His manifest signs in the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, and his protection, care, and the taking of his enemy's mother of him: ﴿perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas: 9]. Fir'awn continued slaughtering the sons, fearing a boy who would demolish his kingdom, until that boy was brought up under his own care, protection and service, so that it would be known to whom the planning and execution belong, and how the enforcement of the prior decree and destiny works. Would that Quraysh had asked, listened, reflected and taken heed: ﴿Has there not come to them clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]. Then He, glorified, followed that with the departure of Musa, peace be upon him, from his land, when he left it fearful and watchful, and what great happiness he, peace be upon him, attained in that departure. In that there is an admonition to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding his departure from Makkah, a consolation for him, and an announcement that the Exalted will return him to his city and grant it to him. With this subtle hint from here, He declared at the end of the surah in His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, He who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely return you to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas: 85]. This is sufficient for what was intended. End of quotation.

Since it was as though someone had asked, "What is this recounted story?", He said: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh﴾, the king of Egypt who claimed divinity, ﴿exalted himself﴾, that is, by his claim to divinity, his tyranny over the servants of God, and his subjugation of them, ﴿in the land﴾ [that is, because We had gathered the armies around him, so they were with him as one single party, and thereby We carried out his word]. (p-239) Although the intended "land" here is the land of Egypt, its unrestricted use indicates its greatness, and that it is like the whole earth in containing what few other lands contain.

[Since the implied meaning conveyed by the conjunction was: "So he denied that blessing," He followed it with His saying:] ﴿And made﴾ [by the power of the word that We had granted him] ﴿its people﴾, that is, the intended land, ﴿into sects﴾, that is, factions, each faction following something and supporting it, while all were under his domination and at his command. They had become with him like kindling, which is splintered firewood. He divided them so that they would not unite against him and so that he would not be prevented from attaining what he wanted from them. [So their word was divided, and they did not defend one another, so they abandoned one another and their affair became base.] The verse is an instance of *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one element is mentioned and its counterpart left implicit, and the implicit counterpart is understood from the mentioned one). It mentions exaltation first as an indication of degradation second, and division second as an indication of unity first. He made them so while he was ﴿oppressing﴾, that is, seeking and bringing about that a group be weakened. Alternatively, this is a new sentence, ﴿a group of them﴾, and they were the Children of Israel, through whom the lives of all the people of Egypt had been secured by the hand of one of them, namely Yusuf, peace be upon him.

He had shown them more kindness than any father shows his son, yet they repaid him, in his children and his brothers, by enslaving them. Then that did not suffice them, until they inflicted upon them, at the hands of this stubborn tyrant, the worst torment. Alas, what a stranger they were among them, both in the past and in the present!

Then God, glory be to Him, explained the oppression with His saying: (p-240) ﴿He slaughters﴾, that is, a great deal of slaughtering, ﴿their sons﴾, that is, at birth. He assigned people to watch for this, so that whenever a woman gave birth to a male, they would slaughter him out of fear for his kingdom, from the assumption that a male among them would be born. ﴿And spares their women﴾, that is, he wanted the women to live, so he did not slaughter them.

Since this was an extremely heinous matter, not commanded by any religious law, and of no benefit at all, for decree, assuming the truthfulness of the one who informed him, cannot be averted by caution, God, Exalted is He, said, explaining its ugliness and elaborating on what his condition implied: ﴿Indeed, he was﴾, that is, as a firmly established state, ﴿among the corrupters﴾, that is, those who have a long-standing record in this attribute. Thus this particular act, which falls under the general matter that is inherent in him, cannot but proceed from him.

When the intended meaning, as the context indicates, was that Pharaoh, asking about the cause of this strange act of his, wanted by it to claim that his rule would last and that none of them would strip him of it, one of his scholars informed him that a man would overcome him and rescue his people from servitude, He joined to it His saying, narrating that past state: ﴿And We wish﴾. It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya), meaning: he oppresses them while the situation is that We intend in the future to strengthen them. That is, he intends the continuation of their oppression, while at the time of Our intention the opposite occurs, namely that We cut that off by the intention of ﴿to bestow favour﴾, meaning: We give, by Our power and knowledge, what is worthy of being a favour ﴿upon those who were deemed weak﴾, meaning: their weakening took place and this shameful act was accepted, and their Lord did not regard them with care ﴿in the land﴾, meaning: the land of Egypt [so they were humbled and abased, and We show them, in themselves and in their enemies, what they love and beyond what they hope] ﴿and make them imams﴾, meaning: leaders in religion and worldly affairs, scholars who call to Paradise, the reverse of the outcome that befell the family of Pharaoh. This is alongside Our making them such that each one of them is fit to aspire to kingship after having been enslaved, being at the utmost remove from it ﴿and make them﴾, by Our might and greatness, ﴿the inheritors﴾, meaning: the heirs to the kingdom of Egypt, with none among the Copts disputing it with them, and to every land We commanded them to aim for. This is a declaration of the destruction of all of them.

(p. 241)

When he gave the good news of their being granted authority within a context that indicated their capability, he stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿And We would establish﴾, i.e., We would bring about the establishment ﴿for them in the earth﴾, i.e., all of it, especially the land of Egypt and the Levant, by destroying their enemies and strengthening them through the Interlocutor of God (Moses), then through the prophets after him, peace be upon them, such that We empower them through their means over others, by what We support them with of angels and by manifesting for them extraordinary signs.

When he mentioned the establishment of authority, he mentioned that it was accompanied by the overcoming of tyrants, to inform that it was the greatest establishment. So he said, [linking it to the sense of: ﴿And We wished to show favour to those who were oppressed in the earth and to make them leaders and to make them inheritors, and to establish them in the earth, and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts what they feared from them﴾, and what follows], saying: ﴿And We would show﴾, i.e., by the majesty We possess, ﴿Pharaoh﴾, i.e., the one from whom this oppression came, ﴿and Haman﴾ (p-٢٤٢) his minister, ﴿and their hosts﴾, who were the means by which they reached what they desired of corruption, ﴿from them﴾, i.e., from the oppressed, ﴿what they used to fear﴾, i.e., with great earnestness on their part, as if it were an instinct, ﴿they used to beware﴾, i.e., they constantly renewed their caution at all times, continually, with utmost diligence and vigour, lest their dominion be taken away by a boy born among them and what follows from that. Al-Baghawi said: "al-hadhar (caution) is guarding oneself against harm."

[The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two contrasting elements are mentioned, each of which is understood from the other): it mentioned the oppression first as an indication of the strength mentioned second, and the feared outcome second as an indication of the desired outcome mentioned first. The secret of this is that it mentioned the consolation and the hope, as an encouragement to patience and to the coming of relief.]

When the intended meaning was: "So what We willed came to pass, and what others willed came to nothing, and We brought forth from the Children of Israel the boy whom Pharaoh feared for his kingdom, and for whose sake he had been slaughtering the sons of the Children of Israel, and We decreed that he be named Moses, because he would be found between water and trees, and We would raise him in the house of the one who feared him and took precautions against him," (the passage) then followed this known decree with the first blessing He bestowed upon those who were oppressed, saying: ﴿And We revealed﴾, that is, We conveyed by Our majesty, by a hidden means, whose nature God alone knows, whether it was an angel or something else, since there is nothing strange about angels speaking to a saint without prophethood, ﴿to the mother of Moses﴾, that is, the one whom We had decreed would be named by this name, and that Pharaoh's destruction and the end of his kingdom would come at his hand, after she had given birth to him and feared that the slaughterers would kill him. ﴿Suckle him﴾, that is, what you were not secure about for him. He made her request to nurse him and her fear of his slaughter a reality by His saying: ﴿But if you fear for him﴾, that is, from them, that he might cry out and be heard and slaughtered. ﴿Then cast him﴾, that is, after you place him in something that protects him from the water, ﴿into the river﴾ [that is, the Nile, and leave off nursing him]. He defined it and named it a yamm, and the yamm is the sea, for its greatness over other rivers in its size and because it comes from Paradise, and because of the benefits that result from it. He departed from the word "sea" (bahr) to "yamm" because the intended meaning in it is more apparent in terms of vastness. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "This is an indication of trust in God. Trust is the pupil of the eye of reliance, the point of the circle of surrender, and the black center of the heart of submission. It has degrees. The first is the degree of despair, which is the servant's despair of contending with decrees, so that he sits down from disputing the divisions, and thus is freed from the error of rash initiative. The second is the degree of security, which is the servant's security against missing what has been decreed and against the diminishing of what has been written, so that he attains the spirit of contentment, and if not, then the eye of certainty, and if not, then the seeking of patience. The third is witnessing the primacy of the Truth [majestic is His majesty], so that he is freed from the trials of what is sought, and from the burdens of protections, and from ascending the stages of means."

﴿And do not fear﴾, that is, let no fear whatsoever arise in you concerning his drowning [or dying from lack of nursing, however long the time], or his being reached by harm. ﴿And do not grieve﴾, that is, let no grief come upon you at the occurrence of his separation from you. Since fear concerns what is expected to befall, and grief concerns what has already befallen, He gave the reason for His prohibition of both matters by His saying, in a nominal sentence indicating permanence and continuity, emphasizing the improbability of its content: ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you﴾, thereby removing the requirement of fear and grief. Then He increased it with a glad tidings that no other glad tidings can equal, by His saying: ﴿and We will make him one of the messengers﴾, that is, of those who are the elite of creation. [The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device of mutual omission): He mentioned nursing first as an indication of its abandonment second, and fear second as an indication of security first. Its secret is that He mentioned the beloved to her, to strengthen her heart and calm her terror.]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 8:

Since the revelation to her (the mother of Musa) was the cause of casting him into the sea, and casting him into the sea was the cause of his being picked up, He said: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾, meaning: she nursed him. When she feared for him, she made for him a chest, coated it with pitch so that water would not penetrate to him, sealed it well, placed him inside it, and cast it into the Nile. It seems that her house was above the house of Pharaoh, so the water carried him to near the house of Pharaoh, where he became entangled in a tree there. Then a group of Pharaoh's people undertook to pick him up. Al-Baghawi said: "Iltiqat (picking up) is the finding of a thing without seeking it."

﴿The family of Pharaoh﴾: they took the chest. When they opened it, they found Musa, peace be upon him, and they loved him, because of the love that Allah Most High placed in them for him. So they adopted him as a son and named him Musa, because they found him ﴿in water and trees﴾ (p-245). "Mu" in their language means water, and "sa" means tree.

Since the final outcome of his affair was their destruction, and since the intelligent person, especially the one who pretends to cleverness, should not undertake anything until he knows its outcome, how much more so when he claims to be a god, He (glorified be He) expressed it with the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah, the lam that indicates the result of an action, whose meaning is causation), mocking Pharaoh, as the explanation of similar usage has passed more than once. This is in His saying: ﴿that it might be for them an enemy﴾, meaning: through their long fear of him, because he would oppose them in their religion and lead them to the truth; ﴿and a grief﴾, meaning: through the loss of their rule, because he would manifest among them the signs by which Allah destroys whomever He wills of them; then He would destroy all their firstborn sons, so that all of the Children of Israel would be delivered from them, and then He would make them all subject to him. Thus Allah would destroy them by drowning at his hand, a destruction of one soul, and grief and wailing would encompass the people of that entire region. This lam, which denotes cause (ta'lil), is used metaphorically (isti'arah) for what its cause produced, the cause they intended, which was adoption and the comfort of the eye, namely destruction. This is like the lion being borrowed for the brave man, so it is applied to him, and it is said: "Zayd is a lion," because his act was like the lion's act. The meaning, by way of mockery, is that they did not take him except for this purpose, since we exempt them from undertaking what they know to be the end of his affair.

Since no one does this act except a foolish, reckless person, or a heedless, forsaken one who hardly succeeds in such matters with either of the two qualities, He said: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers﴾ (p-246), meaning: all of them are of one disposition, ﴿were sinners (khati'in)﴾, meaning: their habit is deliberately committing sins and straying from the goals. So there is nothing strange in their error in raising one whom they slaughter the sons for the sake of, along with the clear indications that he is from the Children of Israel, whose sons they slaughter. In the compilation of al-'Ubab and al-Muhkam, it is said: Abu 'Ubayd said: "Akhta'a and khata'a are two dialects with one meaning." Ibn 'Arafah said: "It is said: khata'a in his religion and akhta'a, when he follows a path of error, intentionally or unintentionally."

Al-Umawi said: "The mukhti' (one who errs) is the one who intends what is right but arrives at something other than it, while the khati' is the one who deliberately does what should not be done." Ibn Zarif said in al-Af'al: "Khati'a al-shay' khat'an and akhta'ahu: he did not hit it (the target)."

When God, exalted is He, related the final outcome of their affair with him, He condensed the two ends of the story into a summary to lighten the matter for the listener, arousing his longing for the detailed explanation of that summary, and hastening the identification of their error, so that their ignorance, which is the root of their wretchedness, would encompass both the beginning and the end of the account. He then reported what was said when they picked him up, saying, in continuation of ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]: ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said﴾, that is, to Pharaoh, when she took him out of the chest. She is the one whom God had decreed to be a source of happiness for her, and she is Asiya daughter of Muzahim, one of the women of the Children of Israel; al-Baghawi transmitted this. ﴿A comfort of the eye for me﴾, that is, through him, ﴿and for you﴾, that is, O Pharaoh.

Since she established for him that he is one through whom eyes are comforted, this resulted in his being spared, and for this reason ... [she] forbade his killing and feared that she would say, "Do not kill him," and he would answer her by taking it literally and then order his killing, while she would be saving him from falling into breaking his promise. So she combined in her speech: ﴿Do not kill him﴾, that is, neither you yourself nor anyone you command to do so. Then she gave a reason for that, or resumed speaking, and said: ﴿Perhaps﴾, that is, it is possible, and it is fitting and suitable, ﴿that he may benefit us﴾, that is, because of what I imagine in him of nobility, even if he had known parents, ﴿or we may take him as a son﴾, if his parents are not known, so that his benefit would be greater, for he is worthy of being honored by kings.

Since all of this was the act of one who does not know, and it is not valid for him to be a god, she stated this explicitly, rebuking whoever obeyed him in claiming that, and said: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, that is, they retracted this statement while the reality was that they ﴿did not perceive﴾, that is, they had no perception at all, because one who has no knowledge except through acquisition is likewise; how much more so when he does not refine his soul through acquiring it, and how much more so when he is sealed upon his heart. Since they were like this, they had no perception of what their affair with him would lead to of tremendous matters that would result in the destruction of the corrupters, so that they might act accordingly, by taking precautions against him in ways that would save them.

[p. 248] When he had told of the state of the one who found him, he told of the state of the one who had been separated from him, and said: "And there became" (i.e., right after the night in which his separation occurred) "the heart of Moses' mother" (i.e., her heart, which her burning increased with longing, fear and grief; and this indicates that she cast him at night) "empty" (i.e., in extreme dread, because of what she was created with of human dispositions), all of the intended meanings that would normally steady the heart having departed from it. Then he connected this, resuming his statement: "if" (i.e., indeed) "she nearly" (i.e., came close) "to disclose" (i.e., there would occur from her the revealing of everything concerning him, speaking openly) "about him" (i.e., about the matter of Moses, peace be upon him, that he was her son and the like), because of the emptiness of her heart from hidden matters and the scattering of her thought into every valley. "Had We not bound" (by Our majesty) "upon her heart" (after We had returned to it the sound meanings We had deposited in it), so that she did not declare it, owing to Our binding upon it, until it became like a sack whose mouth is tied so that nothing of what is in it comes out. Then he gave the reason for the binding with his words: "so that she might be" (i.e., a state that is like an instinct for her) "among the believers" (i.e., those who affirm what God promised concerning his deliverance and his messengerhood, certain of that).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 11:

When he had informed about her concealing him, he followed it with the report of her action in seeking out news of him, whose concealment had driven her mind away. So he said, conjoining it to ﴿And he became [Qur'an 28:10]﴾, ﴿And she said﴾, that is, his mother, ﴿to his sister﴾, that is, after she had come to be in that state, her matter having been hidden from her: ﴿Follow him up﴾, that is, follow his trail and track his news, by land and by sea. (p-249) So she did, ﴿and she watched him from afar﴾, that is, from a distance, without being face to face. For this reason he said: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾, that is, they had no awareness, neither of her watching nor of her being his sister. Rather they were in a state of heedlessness, which is at the furthest remove from the rank of divinity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 12:

When that was one of the causes of his being returned [to his mother], he mentioned, in a circumstantial clause, another cause close to it, saying: ﴿And We had forbidden﴾, that is, We prevented, by Our majesty whose command cannot be contravened and before which everything becomes insignificant, ﴿upon him the wet-nurses﴾, plural of murdiah (wet-nurse), which refers to those hired for suckling from outsiders. That is, We decreed his prohibition from suckling from them. He used the word "forbidding" (tahrim) metaphorically for "prevention," because it is a prevention containing mercy. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': it is a forbidding of prevention, not a forbidding of legislation (tahrim shar').

Since he had nursed from his mother from the time she gave birth to him until the time she cast him into the river (al-yamm), the prohibition did not cover the past time, so he affirmed the prepositional phrase, saying: ﴿from before﴾, that is, before his mother instructed his sister with what she instructed her, and after she cast him in, so that this would be a cause for his return to her. So he refused to suckle from anyone else. They were concerned for him, so his sister came to them and they said to her: "Do you have a wet-nurse whom you can point us to, so that perhaps he will accept her breast?" ﴿So she said﴾, that is, his sister approached him after looking at him and said to them, when she saw them in extreme concern for his suckling, when they offered him the wet-nurses and he refused to nurse from any one of them: ﴿Shall I﴾ show you something you need, in that ﴿I guide you to a household﴾, and she did not say "to a woman," so as to widen the scope of supposition, ﴿who will take charge of him for you﴾, that is, who will take him in, sustain him, and attend to all his needs, including suckling and other things, for your sake. And she increased their eagerness by her saying: ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, that is, their sincerity toward him is firm, and they will not deceive him with any kind of deception. Al-Baghawi said: "Nush (sincerity) is the opposite of ghish (deceit), and it is purifying an action from the impurities of corruption." So with this speech she nearly stated outright that the one pointed to was her mother. They became suspicious of her speech, so she made an excuse, saying that they do this to draw near to [the king] and to earn his affection by means of him, so they accepted that. And this and similar matters are a clarification from Allah, exalted is He, because no one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Him, glorified is He, so it is not valid that anyone else be a god.

When they had settled him into her care, they asked that she direct them (to a nurse). So his sister came with their mother [and We had already prohibited him to be nursed by any other woman, so We made him willing to take her breast]. He took her breast, and they said: "Stay with us." She said: "I cannot leave my house. If you are pleased that I should raise him in my house, (then I will); otherwise I have no need of it," and she showed indifference toward him in order to remove suspicion. They agreed to this, and she returned him to her house. [This verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one part is mentioned and its counterpart omitted): it mentions the prohibition first as evidence for the permission second, and the sister's question second as evidence for their question to her first. Its secret is that mentioning the more remarkable aspect of the matter is more indicative of power.] For this reason, what came before is connected by His saying: ﴿So We returned him﴾, that is, together with this apparent matter of uncovering his secret, which necessitated doubt about his situation, and together with the preceding indications which almost amount to certainty that he was of the Children of Israel: among them, his being cast into the sea in that condition; among them, that the one indicated for nursing him was of the Children of Israel; and among them, that he accepted her breast over the breasts of the Copts and others, by Our hands, which none can overpower, and against which no trick or plot can prevail, from the hand of the enemy who slaughtered infants only in hope of striking him, and of escaping what had been decreed for him in prior knowledge. ﴿To his mother﴾. It was part of God's command, and God prevails over His command, that He caused Moses' enemy to be employed in his upbringing, as al-Razi said, while the enemy was killing the children of the world on his account. Then He gave the reason with His saying: ﴿so that her eye might be cooled﴾, that is, that it might be refreshed and settled, no longer roving in search of him in every direction, and that she might sleep while nursing him and raising him in her house, secure and unafraid. The "coolness of the eye" through his return and her sleep is the opposite of its heat and wakefulness through constant weeping. One says: qarrat ʿaynuhu taqirru (with kasra or fatha) qurratan, and it may be pronounced with damma, and qurūran: it grew cool with joy and its weeping ceased, or it saw what it had been longing for. God cooled his eye and with his eye ('aynihi). A cool eye is qarīra and qārra, and what cools it is qarrat-hu. One says qarra bi-l-makān yaqirru (with fatha or kasra) qarāran, qurūran, qarran, and taqirratan: it remained and settled. The root of "coolness of the eye" is from qurr, which is coldness: that is, it grew cool, so it was healthy and slept, contrary to the heat of its tears. It is also said that it derives from qarār, meaning "my eye came to rest." They say: the tear of joy is cold and the tear of grief is hot. So the meaning of "God cool your eye" is that He makes it cold with joy and hot with grief. This is the view of al-Asma'i. Abu 'Abbas said: it is not as al-Asma'i mentioned; rather every tear is hot. So the meaning of "God cool your eye" is that it meets joy, so it sleeps and its wakefulness ends, and it meets what pleases you; that is, God grants you the utmost of your hope, so that your eye comes to rest from looking at anything else, content and satisfied with what is in your hands. They said: the meaning of their saying "he is the coolness of my eye" is "he is the contentment of my soul," so it is cooled and settled by his nearness and does not look longingly toward anything else. ﴿And not﴾, that is, and so that she would not ﴿grieve﴾, that is, over his separation; ﴿and that she might know﴾, that is, with a knowledge which is the very certainty of the eye, just as she already knew it with the certainty of knowledge, and knowledge of witnessing just as she already knew it as knowledge of the unseen: ﴿that the promise of God﴾, that is, the matter which the Great King, who possesses all perfection in His preservation and sending, had promised her, ﴿is true﴾, that is, it is in the utmost firmness in corresponding to reality.

Since knowledge is the light, the loss of which means no action is sound and no purpose is ordered, He said, conjoining to what is implied (that she thereby came to know by his return the certainty of the eye after the certainty of knowledge): ﴿But most of them﴾, that is, most of the people of Pharaoh and others, ﴿do not know﴾, that is, they have no knowledge at all, so how can they claim what they claim of divinity and greatness over one with whom God is?

When the situation had settled into this pattern, it was known that nothing lay beyond it but goodness and prosperity, along with the honour and dignity of Pharaoh's adopting him. So he (Moses) passed over what lay between him and the age suitable for mission. [And] he said, informing of what came after those circumstances: ﴿And when he reached his full strength﴾, that is, the gathering of his powers and his perfections, ﴿and attained maturity﴾, that is, he became balanced in age, and his firmness was complete with the end of youth. This is from the span of life between twenty-one years and forty-two years. Thus, by this, he was perfected in the good qualities with which We had created him. Al-Razi said: al-Junayd said: "When his intellect was complete, his insight was sound, his conduct was righteous, and the time of his address had come," end of quote.

That is, he reached the limit beyond which a person gains no further natural disposition (gharizah) that was not present in him during youth. Indeed, after that point there remains only a standstill, then decline. ﴿We gave him﴾, that is, as a departure from the customary course (khariq lil-'ada, a miracle), in the manner of his brothers among the prophets, the beginning of natural dispositions which We bestowed upon him without any acquisition at all. ﴿Judgement﴾, that is, a judgement firmly grounded in knowledge, ﴿and knowledge﴾, that is, (p-254) supported by wisdom, as a preparation for his prophethood and as a prodigy (irhas, a sign preceding the mission) of his messengership. We rewarded him with this for the goodness with which We had created him, as a favour and grace from Us. God, glorified is He, chose this age for the mission so that it would be, as has been indicated, among the extraordinary events, because it is at this point that the beginning of the reversal occurs, of which God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whomever We let live long, We reverse him in creation﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68], that is, until the completion of the age of youth. ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68], that is, We bring him to a halt, so that nothing is added after that to his outward or inward powers, and no disposition appears in him that did not already exist, and then he begins to decline. This is God's custom with all the children of Adam except the prophets. For they, at the stage of standstill, are given from the seas of knowledge what description falls short of, without acquisition, but rather as a natural disposition which God implants in them at that time. They are also given strength of body in proportion to that, so at the time of others' reversal, their growth takes place. The same applies to whoever God joins with them among the righteous followers. In Surah Ya-Sin, God willing, will come the complement of this meaning, which God will open, for whoever reflects upon it, to doors of knowledge. For this reason God, exalted is He, said, connecting to what is implied (we did with him that and with his mother as a reward for them for their goodness in sincerely doing what they did, relying on God alone without turning to anything else at all): ﴿And thus﴾, that is, a reward of such magnitude similar to this, (p-255) ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾, that is, all of them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 15:

When he had informed of his being prepared for his prophethood, he informed of that which was the cause of his emigration (hijrah), and it was as if it had been established as a practice (sunnah) after Ibrahim, peace be upon him. So he said: ﴿And he entered the city﴾, that is, the city of Pharaoh, coming from his palace, because he was to him in the position of a son. Ibn Jarir said: it is the city of Memphis (Manf) in Egypt. Al-Baghawi said: it was said: ʿAyn al-Shams (Heliopolis). It was said other than that. ﴿at a time of heedlessness﴾: it was said: at a time of noon (or "a far time"); and it was said other than that. ﴿from its people﴾, that is, to make firm what We had made a cause of his removal from them, purifying him from the company of the wrongdoing people. ﴿And he found therein﴾, that is, in the city, ﴿two men fighting﴾, that is, doing the preliminaries of killing by grappling together along with choking and striking. They were an Israelite and a Copt. Therefore, answering one who seemed to be asking about them while he was looking at them, he said: ﴿This one is of his faction﴾, that is, of the Children of Israel, his people, ﴿and this one is of his enemy﴾, that is, of the Copts. The Children of Israel had gained strength through him, because he was the stepson of the king, although his wet-nurse was from among them; they did not think that the cause of that was the nursing.

(p-256) ﴿So the one from his faction called for his help against the one from his enemy, and Musa struck him﴾, that is, he answered him, and struck (fawakaza) — that is, he thrust and pushed the enemy with his hand, or struck him with the whole of his palm, as if it were a punch (al-kaam), or pushed him with the tips of his fingers. He was a man of great strength (ayd), to whom was given, of the natural and spiritual powers, what no one of the people of that time was given. ﴿And he decided﴾, that is, he carried out the decree which is decree in its true sense, which is death from which no human escapes, ﴿against him﴾, so he killed him and finished with him. Everything that you finish, you have decreed (qadaytahu), and you have decreed against him. This matter remained hidden from the people because of the heedlessness they were in, so no one among them perceived it.

When it was as if it were said: this matter is grave, so what followed from the words of one who had been given judgment and knowledge? It was answered by informing that he regretted it immediately, with his saying: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿This﴾, that is, the act to which the Israelite drew you, ﴿is from the work of Satan﴾, that is, because I was not commanded to it specifically, and it was not my intention, even though the one killed was a disbeliever. Then he informed about the state of Satan with what he knows of him, emphasizing it to urge himself toward intense caution (p-257) and wariness of him, so he said: ﴿Indeed, he is an enemy﴾, and along with being an enemy from whom one must be wary, ﴿he is a misleader﴾, who does not lead to any good at all; and in addition to that, ﴿he is a clear one﴾, that is, his enmity and his misleading are in the utmost clarity; there is no concealment in either of these two.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 16:

When this disbeliever had nothing in him but regret, because he (ﷺ) had not received a specific permission regarding his killing, and he (ﷺ) had reported about him with regret, the souls of the perceptive yearned for seeking forgiveness on his behalf, knowing that it is the custom of the prophets and the people of lofty ranks to regard lapses as grave (istih'am). So they were answered by the report of his hastening to that, with his saying: ﴿He said﴾, and he dropped the particle of address, following the custom of the chosen ones, so he said: ﴿My Lord﴾, i.e., O You who have shown kindness to me.

When the state of one who undertakes something indicates his intention for it, and approval of it, he emphasized his statement to inform that his inner state was other than what his outward state indicated, so he said: ﴿Indeed I have wronged myself﴾, i.e., by undertaking what had not been preceded by a specific permission [idhn] from You regarding it, even though it was permissible.

Since the one brought near may consider the good deed of another to be his own bad deed, he said, as a consequence of that: ﴿So forgive me﴾, i.e., erase this very lapse and its trace, ﴿for me﴾, i.e., for my sake, do not take me to account. ﴿So He forgave him﴾, i.e., He brought about the erasure for that as he asked, out of honor ﴿to him.﴾ Then he gave the reason for that with his saying, pointing out that the attribute of others is nothingness in relation to His attribute, emphasizing that: ﴿Indeed He, He﴾, i.e., alone, ﴿is the Forgiving﴾, i.e., the one who reaches the utmost in the attribute of concealing for everyone who wills, ﴿the Merciful﴾, i.e., the one of great mercy through kindness, by granting success to deeds pleasing to the station of divinity. And because this is His attribute, He returned him to Pharaoh and his people when He sent him to them, so they were not able to hold him to account for that by retaliation or otherwise, after He had saved him from them before the mission, in a manner beyond analogy.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 28, verse 17:

When Allah, glorified is He, bestowed upon him by granting his request, the listener yearned to hear of his gratitude for it, so he was answered with his saying: ﴿My Lord﴾, that is, O You who have done me every kindness. And since making one thing a recompense for another establishes it more firmly and makes it more fitting for the resolve to be carried out, he said: ﴿by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, that is, because of Your bestowing upon me forgiveness and other things. And since he was in the context of magnifying the blessing, he repeated the particle of causation (bi-ma, "by what") for emphasis and to make clear that what is attached to it is caused by the bestowal. He joined it to the particle of negation that indicates emphasis, and said: ﴿So I will never be a supporter (ẓahīr) for the criminals﴾, that is, a companion (ʿashīr), or an associate (khalīṭ), or a helper (muʿīn), ﴿for the criminals﴾, that is, those who sever what Allah has commanded to be joined. That is, I will not be among the people of the Copts, for their corruption is great, and their oppression of Your servants, the sons of Your friends, is continuous and grave. I have no power to abandon their support, and that would lead to the like of this deed, so I am not fit to be among them. Thus he is not suitable for migrating to them. And this (p-259) is from the saying of the Arabs: "He came to us in his ẓuhrah" (with a ḍammah, with a kasrah, and with a fatḥah) and "ẓāhirah," that is, his clan.

When he mentioned the killing and followed it with what matters more, which is his concern with the Hereafter, he mentioned what resulted from it of the affairs of this world, saying: ﴿So he became﴾, i.e., Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿in the city﴾, i.e., the one in which he had killed the man, ﴿fearful﴾, i.e., because of his killing of him, ﴿watching anxiously﴾, i.e., constantly bound by fear, looking about often with his neck turned, in dread of some visitation that might come upon him in that state. Al-Baghawi said: "Al-taraqqub is awaiting what is disliked."

﴿Then when﴾, i.e., there confronted him ﴿the one who had sought his help﴾, i.e., had asked him for support against his own people ﴿the day before﴾, i.e., the day that followed the day of the earlier appeal for help, ﴿crying out to him﴾, i.e., seeking what would remove the harm for which he was crying out, from another Copt who was wronging him. It was as if it was said: "What did Musa say to him after he had brought him into what he disliked?" So it was said: ﴿Musa said to him﴾, i.e., to this one who was crying out for help, ﴿...﴾

Since the situation required that this Israelite would remain for a period without disputing with anyone, out of fear of the consequences of that man's killing, he emphasized his statement: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly misguided﴾, i.e., one of manifest, extreme error, ﴿evidently﴾, i.e., plainly in error, not hidden in it, because what happened the day before did not keep you from quarreling with one you cannot withstand, even though you were wronged. Then he approached them both in order to help him.

[Then he said], indicating by the fa' (then) the haste to come to his aid: ﴿So when﴾ — and he affirmed the particle whose origin is the verbal noun, for emphasis on the meaning of desire, and said: ﴿he intended﴾, i.e., wished, sought and aimed, confirming that by walking ﴿to strike﴾, i.e., Musa, upon him be peace, ﴿the one who is an enemy to both of them﴾, i.e., from the Copts, by seizing him with violence and force in order to rescue the Israelite from him. ﴿He said﴾, i.e., the Israelite, the one in error, because of what he saw of his anger and what he said to him of harsh words, thinking that he had only approached intending to strike him, him (the Israelite), because of what he had brought upon him, and not his enemy: ﴿O Musa﴾, specifying him by his proper name, to remove every ambiguity, denying the deed which he believed had been done when he saw him approaching them angry while blaming him. ﴿Do you intend to kill me﴾, i.e., today, while I am among your partisans, ﴿as you killed a soul yesterday﴾, i.e., from among the partisans of our enemies. And what shows that the Israelite is the one who said this to him is the context, by the fact that the speech was with him, by what was indicated by entering the city at a time of heedlessness, since no one saw him except the Israelite, and by his saying ﴿an enemy to both of them﴾, which is a censure of the Israelite, as Musa, upon him be peace, stated explicitly.

When he (the Israelite) informed on him and disclosed what no one else knew, he (Musa) feared his harm, so he increased the incitement against him, emphasizing with his saying: ﴿You intend only to be﴾, i.e., that you remain firmly ﴿a tyrant﴾, i.e., dominant and overpowering. Abu Hayyan said: "It is the nature of a tyrant to kill without right."

﴿in the land﴾, i.e., the land in which you are, so that none is above you. ﴿And you do not intend﴾, i.e., a new intention does not arise in you, ﴿to be﴾, i.e., with what is for you like a natural disposition, ﴿among the reformers﴾, i.e., those who excel in reform, for the one who reconciles between people does not reach killing in this manner. So when the man of Pharaoh heard this, he left the Israelite. When that Copt was killed, they suspected the Children of Israel, and they incited Pharaoh against them, and he said: "Is there any evidence?" For the king, even if he is the elite among his people, should not impose punishment without evidence or certainty, as mentioned in the hadith of the one who was deceived, which Abu Ya'la narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Thus, when this one in error uttered this statement, the matter became certain regarding Musa, upon him be peace.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 20:

Since the implied structure of the discourse, as indicated by the context, is: "When the Pharaonic man heard the words of the Israelite, he left him. Then the speech continued until it reached Pharaoh, and the discussion came to concern the command to kill Musa, peace be upon him," he connected it with His words: ﴿And a man came﴾, that is, from among those who love Musa, peace be upon him. And since the matter was important and required great resolve and immense strength, he placed the doer of the coming (the subject) before its complement, unlike what occurs in Surah Ya-Sin.

Since the verse is concerned with demonstrating power over tremendous affairs, from seizing a person by the throat until one says, "There is no escape," and then rescuing him with relief until one says, "There is no destruction," he described the man, saying: ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾, that is, the most distant of its places. He made clear that he was walking by saying: ﴿hastening﴾. [But] he took a shortcut and hurried in his walking, to the extent that he was running, so he outpaced them by his great effort in hastening and by renewing his resolve at every moment of his hastening. It is as if it were said: "What did he do?" So it was said: ﴿He said﴾, calling him by his name, out of tenderness and to remove any confusion: ﴿O Musa﴾. He emphasized, to indicate that the matter had come upon them suddenly and that the time does not allow for detailed inquiry, so he said: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs﴾, that is, the nobles of the Copts (al-Qibt) who hold the power to bind and loosen, because they have the capacity to command and forbid, ﴿are conferring about you﴾, that is, they are consulting about your case, until their situation in their consultation reached the point that each of them commands the other and is commanded by his order. It is as if it were said: "Why do they do that?" So it was said: ﴿to kill you﴾, because they heard that you had killed their companion. ﴿So leave﴾, that is, leave this city. Then he gave the reason for that, by way of emphasis, in order to remove any possibility that the killing would not occur because of his high standing with the king, saying: ﴿Indeed I am for you﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿among the sincere advisers﴾, that is, those who are most firm in their sincerity.

**Then he left it** (*fa-kharaja*), i.e. Musa, upon him be peace, hastening **from it** (*minhā*), i.e. the city, because he knew the truthfulness of what he had been told, given the indications that surrounded it, **while being fearful** (*khā'ifan*) **for his own self from the people of Pharaoh**, **looking about watchfully** (*yataraqqab*), i.e. turning his head often in every direction, looking to see whether anyone was following him. Then he joined to this, by way of resumption (*istiʾnaf*), his saying: **He said**, i.e. Musa, upon him be peace: **"My Lord"** [i.e.: O You who do good to me by bringing me into being, by nurturing me, and by other forms of kindness], **"deliver me"** (*najjini*), i.e. rescue me. It is derived from *al-najwah*, which is an elevated place that not everyone can reach. **"from the wrongdoing people"**, i.e. those who place matters in other than their proper places, killing one who does not deserve to be killed despite their power. So God answered him and guided him to take the major road toward Madyan, and that was the cause of his deliverance. This is because those who were dispatched after him were certain that he would not take the main road, following the habit of fearful fugitives of walking *ʿusafan* (without a set direction, off the beaten path) or of taking the narrow tracks of the road. So they turned to the right and left in what they assumed, and thus they missed him.

When he had made this supplication, God, exalted is He, informed of its being answered, telling of the direction of his intent, for added benefit, so He said: ﴿And when﴾, that is: so God answered his supplication, rescued him from them, and directed him toward Madyan. And when he ﴿turned toward﴾, that is: he set his face, intending ﴿the way of﴾ [that is: the road] which leads its traveler to the land of ﴿Madyan﴾, the city of God's Prophet Shu'ayb, upon whom be prayers and peace, his heart turned toward his Lord, ﴿he said﴾, that is, because he (p-264) did not know the road: ﴿"Perhaps"﴾, that is: it is fitting, deserving, and certain.

Since his devotion to God was most complete, owing to his great watchfulness (muraqaba) over Him, he said, placing it first: ﴿"My Lord"﴾, that is: the One who does good to me by great nurture in matters of destruction, ﴿"that He may guide me to the right"﴾, that is: the just and middle ﴿"path"﴾, which is the road that makes him perceive it without crookedness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 23:

Since the implied sense is: "So he reached the city," he followed it with His words: ﴿And when he arrived﴾, meaning Musa, upon him be peace, arrived as one who comes to drink from ﴿the water of Madyan﴾, that is, the water from which the shepherds give drink. ﴿He found upon it﴾, that is, upon the water, ﴿a community﴾, that is, a large group, ﴿of people﴾, who are fit to be sought and to seek, and therefore they were dominant and prevailing over the water. Then He specified their kind by His words ﴿of people﴾, and He also specified their activity by His words ﴿watering﴾, that is, their livestock. He omitted the object because it is not intended; what is intended is the act itself, and likewise what follows it. For his mercy, upon him be peace, was not because the animals driven away and watered were sheep, but because of driving away in general and leaving the watering undone. ﴿And he found besides them﴾, that is, a finding that began from a place nearest to their location as they came to the water, ﴿two women﴾. He expressed it this way because, when He made them, glorified is He, people of manliness (muruwwah, chivalry) and noble character, as one will know who reflects carefully on what is related about them, ﴿driving back﴾, that is, they were exercising the driving back (dhawd), which is restraining, preventing and holding back, and undertaking the lesser of two harms, so they restrained their flocks when the flock was pushed toward the crowd by thirst, lest it be mixed with the people's flocks.

Since this situation necessarily called for asking about it, it was as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" It was said: ﴿He said﴾ [that is:] Musa, upon him be peace, out of mercy toward them: ﴿What is your matter?﴾, that is, your news and your matter (makhtub), that is, what you seek, and this is like expressing the affair by the thing concerned that deserves to be addressed because of its greatness, namely your driving back your flocks from watering. Abu Hayyan said: "Asking about a matter (al-khatb) is only in cases of calamity or oppression."

Since it was known that his question was about the cause, ﴿They both said﴾ [that is:] by way of apology for their condition and as a hint of their need for help: ﴿We cannot﴾ [that is:] inform us that we do not ﴿water﴾, that is, our flocks, and He omitted the object because it is known, ﴿until the shepherds send back﴾, that is, depart and return ﴿from the water﴾, lest they mix with them. This is according to the reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir with a fatha on the ya' [and a damma on the dal], as a triliteral verb. The meaning according to the reading of the rest, with a damma and a kasra, is that they cause the sending back and the turning away.

Since the implied sense is: "Because we are women," and since the context, given their young age, requires that they have a father and no brothers, otherwise these would have spared them this, they connected to this implied clause their words: ﴿And our father is an old man, very aged﴾, that is, he cannot water because of his old age, so we were compelled to what you see. This is also an apology for their father having sent them for this, because it is not forbidden, so religion does not reject it. People differ in this according to manliness, and their customs in it vary, and the conditions of the Arabs and the Bedouins differ from those of the non-Arabs and the settled people, especially when necessity calls for it.

﴿So he watered [their flock] for them﴾, that is, Musa, peace be upon him, for them, when he knew their need, seizing the opportunity for reward and the nobility of character in helping the weak, despite the fatigue and hunger he himself was suffering. ﴿Then he turned back﴾, that is, Musa, peace be upon him, withdrew, making his back face what had been facing him, ﴿to the shade﴾, that is, so that he might rest beneath it and take repose, turning in devotion to the Creator after having discharged his advice to the creatures. He knew of the shade because it is known that a spot is hardly ever without something that casts shade, especially places of water. ﴿And he said﴾, for there is no deficiency in complaining to the Exalted Master, the absolutely Self-Sufficient, ﴿My Lord﴾.

Since his condition in his great patience was that of one who does not ask, he emphasized his request, to make known his intense longing for what he asked for and to add to the supplication and tenderness. So he said: (p-267) ﴿Indeed I﴾, and he emphasized his neediness by attaching it with the preposition لِ (li) rather than إلى (ila), so he said: ﴿for whatever﴾, that is, for any thing. Since the provision that comes to a human being is a consequence of the decree that comes from the Most High, the Great, he expressed it with the verb of sending down and expressed it in the past tense, to generalize the state of neediness and to affirm the fulfilment of the promise of provision, so he said: ﴿You have sent down﴾. Perhaps he omitted the returning pronoun for brevity, due to the weariness he was suffering: ﴿to me of good﴾, that is, even if it is little. ﴿Needy﴾, that is, one in distress. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the harm had reached such a point that his belly had turned green from eating herbs and he had become so weak that his stomach stuck to his back.

So look at these two Prophets, peace be upon them, in their state of need, and they are the best of that age, so that you may have in that an example, and take him as a leader and a model, and say: "O my father and mother! What the Prophets and the righteous suffered of hardship and calamities in the prison of this world," as a means of protecting them from it and honouring them by their Lord, raising their ranks in His sight, and treating it with contempt, even though the ignorant deceived one may think otherwise. In the story there is encouragement to good, exhortation to help one another in righteousness, and an incitement to give kindness with effort.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 25:

When the hearing of the two women of his speech, together with his kindness toward them, became the cause of Shu'ayb's (peace be upon him) invitation to him, [the author] said, building upon what is implied: "So the two women went to their father and told him of their news and of his kindness toward them, so he commanded that he be invited, that he might reward him: ﴿Then one of them came to him⦆ — that is, by the father's word, and immediately — ﴿one of them﴾ — that is, of the two women (p-268) — ﴿walking⦆ — and since modesty (ḥayāʾ) is like a mount for her, over which she is firmly seated, holding its reins, he expressed it with the particle of elevation, saying: ﴿with bashfulness⦆ — that is, with an existing modesty on her part, because she was charged with coming to a foreign man, speaking to him and walking beside him. Then he resumed the report about what the listener was eager to know of her affair, saying: ﴿She said⦆, and emphasized it to inform of her father's desire to meet him, in her saying: ﴿Indeed my father⦆, and she depicted his state with the present tense, saying: ﴿invites you, that he may reward you⦆ — that is, give you a recompense for you, because recompense is one of the traits of the noble, and accepting it carries no shame — ﴿the wage for what you watered for us⦆ — that is, our livestock. So he hastened to respond, because of the harmony between them. For this reason he said: ﴿Then when⦆ with the fāʾ (so) ﴿he came to him⦆ — that is, Moses came to Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both — ﴿and related⦆ — that is, Moses (peace be upon him) — ﴿to him⦆ — that is, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) — ﴿the stories⦆ — that is, he narrated to him his account with Pharaoh and his household, regarding their disbelief, their tyranny, and their humiliation of God's servants, and he traced out the matters for him as they truly were, since he discerned in him what God had given him of judgment and knowledge, of sincere counsel and compassion, of knowledge and wisdom, and of majesty and greatness.

Since it is well known that there is no life for one who is afraid, and since security is what a person needs most, he presented him with reassurance by saying: ﴿He said⦆ — that is, Shu'ayb said to him, peace be upon them both: ﴿Do not fear⦆ — [that is:] for Pharaoh has no authority over you here (p-269), and because God's custom has been [that] your humility of this kind has never existed in anyone except that God decreed his elevation. For this reason the outcome was: ﴿You have escaped⦆ — that is, O Moses — ﴿from the wrongdoing people⦆ — that is, he and others, even though they were at the utmost strength and ancient standing in wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 26:

When this statement implied that he had taken him into his care, his two daughters understood its substance. Both of them had seen his sufficiency (kifayah) and his trustworthiness (diyanah), which encouraged them toward his company. So the soul became eager for their circumstances at that time, and he said, resuming on that matter: ﴿One of the two women said﴾, i.e., of the two women. It was said: she is the one who called him to their father, indicating with the vocative particle of distance (ya', as in "ya abati") her belittling of herself and the great rank of her father: ﴿O my father, hire him﴾ so that he may suffice us in what concerns us. Then she gave a reason for her statement, saying, emphasizing it to show her eagerness for good and her satisfaction with it: ﴿Indeed the best of those you hire﴾ for anything at all ﴿is the strong﴾, and this is him, because of what we have seen of his strength in watering (the flocks), ﴿the trustworthy﴾, because of what we have discerned in him of modesty and chastity in his gaze, his speech, his actions, and all his other conditions. Abu Hayyan said: Her statement is the words of a wise person, comprehensive, for when trustworthiness and sufficiency are combined in the one who undertakes a matter, the purpose is accomplished.

﴿He said﴾ [i.e., ] Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. In the Torah he is called Ra'ū'īl, with a fatḥah on the rā', a ḍammah on the unmarked ʿayn, a sukūn on the wāw, then a kasrah on the hamzah followed by a sukūn on the yā', and an lām. He is also called Yithrū, with a fatḥah on the yā', a sukūn on the unmarked thāʾ, a ḍammah on the unmarked rā', and a sukūn on the wāw. ﴿Indeed, I intend﴾ O Mūsā. The emphasis (on the intention) is because a stranger is rarely desired at first arrival, especially by leaders, so the desire must be stated in full. ﴿to marry you﴾ i.e., to give you in marriage, a marriage whose bond is like the joining of one jaw to the other. ﴿one of my two daughters﴾

Since it was possible that the one to be married might be someone other than the two whose water he had drawn, he negated this with His words: ﴿these two﴾, i.e., the two present, for whom you watered (the flocks), so that he may consider them and see which of them he chooses, and then he will contract the marriage with her. ﴿on condition that you work for me﴾ i.e., that you make yourself a hired worker for me, or that you make my payment for that and my reward. ﴿eight years﴾ The plural of ḥijjah (with a kasrah), meaning years. That is, the work in them is that you be a hired worker for me, and I will employ you in what concerns me of tending the sheep and other matters. The verb ājara (with or without the long vowel) is from ajr and ījār. Likewise, ājara the hired worker and the slave means he gave them their wages. ﴿But if you complete﴾ i.e., the eight by reaching the completion of the contract, by making it ﴿ten﴾, i.e., ten years. ﴿then it is from﴾ i.e., that is a favor ﴿from your own﴾ (self), not obligatory upon you. The specification of eight was because, if the period of pregnancy is subtracted from it, it is the least age at which a child can generally be distinguished, while ten is the least age at which puberty can occur, so that he may look upon his grandson, if he is able, and judge him by what he sees of his speech and conduct. The expression with what is derived from ḥajj (pilgrimage, which means intending a destination) is an omen that the years will be good, that in each of them there will be obedience to God's command, abundance of provision, outpouring of blessings, and warding off of afflictions, and that each of them will be worthy of being sought, or that in each of them there will be a pilgrimage to the Sacred House of God.

When he mentioned this to him, he wished to inform him that after the condition, the matter between them was based on leniency, so he said: ﴿And I do not intend to burden you﴾, i.e., to put you to hardship in any of that or anything else, whether obligatory or not. Then he emphasized the meaning of leniency by stressing the promise of good companionship, so he said: ﴿You will find me﴾. Then he added an exception, following the practice of God's friends and His prophets in referring the matter to Him as a way of humility, so he said: ﴿if God wills﴾, i.e., the One to whom belongs the whole command, ﴿among the righteous﴾, i.e., in good companionship, in fulfilling what you have said, and in every good you desire.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 28:

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said): i.e., Mūsā (upon him be peace). ﴿Dhālika﴾ (That): i.e., what I have mentioned of the choice and other terms. ﴿Baynī wa-baynaka﴾ (between me and you): i.e., it is in force between us upon the basis of equity, justice and fairness, regarding what you have obligated me to as a binding requirement, and what you alluded to of bestowing a favor as a kindness, while upon you is what you have obligated yourself to as a duty and a bounty. (p-272) Then he clarified and explained that by his saying: ﴿Ayyamā al-ajalayni﴾ (Whichever of the two terms): i.e., whichever term of them: the eight or the ten. ﴿Qaḍaytu﴾ (I fulfill): i.e., you carry out the work stipulated upon me in it, and by it you are released from the obligation. ﴿Fa-lā ʿudwāna﴾ (then there is no transgression): i.e., no aggression on account of that against you or against anyone ﴿ʿalayya﴾ (upon me) [i.e.,] in seeking more than it, because just as an increase beyond the ten is not obligatory, so an increase beyond the eight is not obligatory upon me. It seems that by negating the intensive form (ʿudwān as a hyperbolic form), he indicated that, because of the breadth of his chest and the purity of his character, he would not be held to account even for the mere enmity (of any kind). ﴿Wa-Allāhu﴾ (And God): i.e., the Supreme King ﴿ʿalā mā naqūlu﴾ (is over what we say): i.e., all of it, at this time and at other times. ﴿Wakīl﴾ (is Guardian): i.e., a witness and a preserver, dominant over it and holding it binding, in this world and in the Hereafter. So what, then, is to be supposed about what has passed between us of the covenant, of the marriage, of the wage and of the term?

The Torah (the Jewish scripture, the Pentateuch) mentions the content of this. In the beginning of its second book it says: "These are the names of the children of Israel who came into Egypt with Jacob, each man and his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. The number of Jacob's descendants who came out of his loins was seventy souls, together with Joseph, who was in Egypt. Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation. The children of Israel multiplied, bore children, grew numerous, and became very, very mighty, and the land was filled with them. Then a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph, and he said to his people: 'This people, the children of Israel, have become more numerous and mightier than us. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them before they multiply, lest, if war befalls us, they join our enemies, fight against us, and drive us out of the land.' So he set over them taskmasters of harshness and cruelty to afflict them with labour, and they began building for Pharaoh's storehouses and granaries. (In one copy: they built for Pharaoh fortified cities, namely Pithom and Raamses, at al-Fayyum, in 'Ayn Shams; and in another copy: Pithom and Ra'musis; and in another copy: Akwan, which is the City of the Sun.) Their servitude and oppression grew severe, and they increased in number and grew mighty. Their distress and sorrow increased because of the children of Israel. The Egyptians subjected the children of Israel to servitude with severity and harshness, and they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, with clay, with brickmaking, and with all kinds of labour in the field. Their servitude of them, in everything they made them do, was with severity, harshness and cruelty. The king of Egypt said: '[And We appointed] for the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was called Shiphrah and the other Puah, and he commanded them: When you attend the Hebrew women, look at the birth stool; if it is a son, kill him, and if it is a daughter, let her live.' But the midwives feared God and did not do what the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they let the boys live. The king of Egypt summoned the two midwives and said to them: 'Why have you done this? You have disobeyed my command and let the boys live?' They said to Pharaoh: 'The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are midwives and give birth before the midwife reaches them.' God dealt well with the two midwives for this deed. The people multiplied and became very mighty. And when the midwives feared God, He gave them households, and in another copy: houses. Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying: 'Every son that is born to them, cast him into the river, and every daughter, let her live.' A man of the house of Levi went and married a daughter of Levi. The woman conceived and bore a son, and she saw that he was beautiful, so she hid him for three months, and she could not hide him longer than that. She took an ark of cypress wood, daubed it with bitumen and pitch, placed the child in it, and set it in the reeds on the bank of the river. His sister stood at a distance to see what would become of him. Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe in the river, and she saw the ark in the reeds, so she sent her maids, who brought it, and she opened it and saw the child; and behold, he was crying, and she had compassion on him and said: 'This is one of the Hebrew children.' His sister said to Pharaoh's daughter: 'Shall I go and call for you a Hebrew woman to nurse this child?' Pharaoh's daughter said to her: 'Yes, go.' The girl went and called the child's mother. Pharaoh's daughter said to her: 'Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.' The woman took the child and nursed him. When the child grew up, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and she adopted him and named him Moses, because she said: 'I drew him out of the water.' When those days had passed, Moses grew up and went out to his brethren and looked at their burdens. He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew man of his brethren, the children of Israel. He looked this way and that and saw no one, so he killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand. Then he went out another day, and behold, two Hebrew men were quarrelling. He said to the one in the wrong: 'Why do you strike your brother?' He said: 'Who made you a prince and judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?' Moses feared and said: 'Surely this matter has become known.' When the matter reached Pharaoh, he sought to kill Moses, but Moses fled from Pharaoh and went to the land of Midian, and sat down by a well. The priest of Midian had seven daughters, who came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock. The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses rose up, defended them, and watered their flock. They came to Reuel their father, and he said to them: 'Why have you come back so soon today?'
