They said: 'An Egyptian man rescued us from the hands of the shepherds, drew water for us, and watered our flock.' He said to his daughters: 'Where is he? Why have you left the man? Go and call him, that he may eat bread with us.' They did so, and Moses was content to dwell with that man, and he gave him Zipporah his daughter in marriage. She bore him a son, and he named him Gershom, because he said: 'I have become a stranger in a foreign land.' She bore him another son, and he named him Eliezer, because he said: 'The God of my fathers helped me and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.'"

As for his saying that the two quarrelling men on the second day were Hebrews: if the Qur'anic text can be applied to it, well and good; otherwise it is among what they altered. And his saying that the daughters of Shu'ayb were seven does not contradict the noble Qur'an. Indeed, al-Zamakhshari supported it by specifying the two with his words "these two" (in the Qur'an), but the preceding mention indicates that this is not necessary.

Since it is known that the sense is: when Moses, peace be upon him, undertook to marry him his daughter as he had stipulated, and remained with him until he had fulfilled what was incumbent upon him, He followed it with His words: ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term﴾, meaning he completed and finished it, and ﴿Moses﴾ carried out ﴿the term﴾ with his companion, meaning the fuller and more complete term, which is ten years, by fulfilling all that he had stipulated of work. For it has been reported that he fulfilled the better of the two terms, and married the younger of the two daughters, who is the one who came and said: "O my father, hire him" (narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat with this meaning, from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that he stayed with him after the term as well for a period, because he connected with the particle "wa" (and) his saying: ﴿and he set out﴾, and did not make it a response to "when" (lamma). ﴿With his family﴾, meaning his wife, returning to his relatives in Egypt. ﴿He perceived﴾, meaning he saw ﴿from the side of the mount a fire﴾, which its sight made him feel at ease and its brightness illuminated him, and he was in need of guidance to the path and of warming himself by the fire.

Since it was as if it were said: What did he do when he saw it? It was said: ﴿He said to his family﴾. And since women are the thing most fitting to conceal, he addressed them with masculine pronouns, saying: ﴿Wait﴾. Even if his sons were with him, this is by way of predominance. Then he gave the reason for that with his emphatic words, to make it unlikely that there would be a fire in that barren place, at that time of intense cold: ﴿Surely I have perceived a fire﴾. It was as if it were said: What will you do with it? So he said, expressing it with hope, since that is more fitting to humility, which is the purpose of the surah, and is the reality in the perception of human beings in such a situation, and for this reason he expressed it with "a brand", whose basic meaning is steadiness: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it﴾, meaning from its place, ﴿news﴾ that will benefit us in showing the way to the goal, ﴿or a brand﴾, meaning a thick stick, ﴿from the fire﴾, meaning one in which this reality is established, or which was mentioned before. Then he resumed his words: ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾, meaning so that you may be hopeful of coming close to the fire and bending over it to be warmed, and this is evidence that the time was winter.

﴿When he came to it﴾, i.e., the fire.

Since the final part of the speech clearly indicates that the caller is Allah, the Exalted, He used the passive form, ﴿was called﴾, which points to what was hidden at the beginning of the matter. His call, glory be to Him, does not resemble the call of anyone else, but comes from all directions. Yet some places may be specially honored by a particular attribute, either because it is the first place where the call is heard or for some other reason, or because of Musa's (peace be upon him) status. He said, ﴿from﴾, i.e., Musa (peace be upon him) being near ﴿the shore﴾, i.e., the side, ﴿of the valley﴾, on the right of Musa (peace be upon him). For this reason He said ﴿the right﴾, which is an attribute of the shore, that is, being on it, or being, ﴿in the blessed spot﴾, being at the beginning or the main part of the call, or Musa (peace be upon him) being [near] ﴿the tree﴾. This is like when you say: "I called so-and-so from his house." Perhaps the tree was large. When he reached it, the light entered from its edge to its middle, so he entered after it until he was in its midst, and he heard, while within it, the speech of Allah the Exalted in reality. He is the One who speaks, glory be to Him, and not the tree. Al-Qushayri said: "The summary of the consensus (ijma') is that he (peace be upon him) heard the speech of Allah that night. Had that been the call of the tree, the speaker would have been the tree." Al-Taftazani, in his commentary on al-Maqasid, said: "The view preferred by Hujjat al-Islam (the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali) is that he heard His eternal speech without sound or letters, just as His essence will be seen in the Hereafter, without quantity or modality." Earlier, in Surah Ta-Ha, it was mentioned that the intended direction is the one on the right of someone facing from Egypt toward the Noble Ka'bah. As for the tree, al-Baghawi said: Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It was a green acacia (samurah) that shone." Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "It was a thorny bush (awsajah)." Wahb said: "It was from the ʿalīq (a kind of climbing plant)." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "It was the jujube (ʿunnab)."

Then He mentioned the one being addressed with His words: ﴿That O Musa﴾, and He emphasized it, because He, glory be to Him, in His greatness, makes everyone consider themselves unworthy to be addressed by Him, especially at the beginning of the matter. So He said: ﴿Indeed I am Allah﴾, i.e., the One who possesses the most beautiful names and the highest attributes.

Since this name is hidden, He made Himself known by an attribute that gathers the actions observable to humans, so He said: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, i.e., the Creator of all creatures and their Sustainer.

﴿And throw down your staff﴾, that is, so that I may show you a sign in it.

Since the implied sense is: so he threw it, and it immediately became a great serpent, and although it was enormous, it was extremely swift, he built on this his saying: ﴿When he saw it﴾, that is, the staff, ﴿moving swiftly as if it were a jann﴾, that is, in its speed and agility, ﴿a small serpent﴾, ﴿he turned and fled, retreating in fear of it, and did not look back toward it﴾. This is the meaning of his saying: ﴿and did not turn back﴾, that is, Moses, peace be upon him. That is a kinaya (metonymy) for the intensity of his determination to flee and to hasten in fleeing, out of fear of being overtaken in pursuit. So it was said to him: ﴿O Moses, come forward﴾, that is, turn back and advance toward it, ﴿and do not fear﴾. Then the command was emphasized for him, because of what the human being is naturally disposed to in terms of aversion, even if he believes the report to be true, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the secure﴾, that is, those who are foremost in security, as is the custom of your brother messengers.

Then He increased his reassurance by His saying: ﴿Insert﴾, that is, enter [your hand] with steadiness together with ease and nimbleness, ﴿your hand into your bosom﴾, that is, the opening in your garment through which the head comes out, or it is the sleeve, just as a thread (*silk*, the string on which pearls are strung) passes through. [Your hand] will come out in its own color and in the state it was in, free of the trace of the burn which Pharaoh could not cure. He brought it out. ﴿It will come out white﴾, that is, a great whiteness that will have an extraordinary status, beyond the customary. ﴿Without any evil﴾, that is, without any defect from a burn or otherwise. So it came out with a radiance like the light of the sun. The verse is therefore of the type called *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one part of a pair is left implied, the other being stated).

Since this would not be a confirmed sign, given the absence of any defect, unless it returned after that to the color of the body, He said: ﴿And draw your arm close to you﴾, that is, to your body. Since the context concerns securing [Moses] from fear, He expressed it with *janah* (wing), because a bird is safe when it folds its wing. So He said: ﴿your wing﴾, that is, your two hands, which have become white. What is meant by *janah* (wing) in the verse of Ta-Ha is the armpit and the side, because it is a shared term (*mushtarak*, a word with several meanings). ﴿From fear﴾, that is, from dread lest you think it is defective, emerging as it was before its whiteness in the color of your body. This is according to the view that the fear meant by *rahb* is the terror that overwhelmed him and made him flee. It is also possible that what is meant by *rahb* is the sleeve, so that putting the hand into the opening, which is not its proper place but rather the head, is for whiteness, and putting it into the sleeve, which belongs to it, is for its return to its usual state. In al-Baghawi, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both), that Allah Most High commanded him to press his hand to his chest, and his fear caused by seeing the serpent departed from him. He said: "No one who is afraid, after Musa (peace be upon him), places his hand on his chest without his fear leaving him." He stated the word *janah* (wing) explicitly, without a pronoun, to magnify the occasion and to draw attention to the fact that its return to its original state is an independent sign. He expressed it by the word *janah* (wing) to draw attention to gratitude by magnifying its benefit.

When its being a sign was complete, through its turning white and then returning to its color, He said: ﴿Those two﴾, that is, the staff and the white hand. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Ruways read *fa-dhaanika* with the doubled consonant (*shaddah*), to strengthen it so that it would be equal to the fully declinable nouns (*al-asma' al-mutamakkinah*). He used the masculine to add to the strengthening. ﴿Are two proofs﴾, that is, two authorities and two overpowering arguments ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One who does you good, whom no one other than Him can match with the like of them ﴿to﴾, that is, reaching out, or you are sent with them ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ whenever you want that, you will find them, not that they will be yours only here in this pit. Then He gave the reason for sending [Moses] to them, in terms of showing the signs to them and their continuance, by His saying, emphasizing it as a reminder that his proceeding to return to them is the act of one who supposes that they have turned back from their error, and as an announcement of His favor to him in protecting him from them through these proofs: ﴿Indeed they were﴾, that is, by nature and disposition ﴿a people﴾, that is, powerful ones ﴿defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, departing from obedience. So when they see that, they will be awed by you, and they will not be able to reach you with harm, while you will be in a position to turn them back from their defiance.

(p-283) Since it was as if it were said: "What did he do after seeing these marvels?" It was said: "He stood firm, knowing the difficulty of the situation and the gravity of the matter, so he made a condition for himself until he was content. Such was his habit: steadfastness and resolve, forbearance and knowledge. Do you not see what he did with us, peace and salutations and honour be upon him, of goodness on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), in asking for the lightening of the prayer? And for all of that, ﴿He said: "My Lord"﴾, that is: O You who have done good to me, ﴿"indeed I"﴾ — he emphasised it because God's sending him is the act of one who does not regard that they have a claim (tirah, i.e., a blood-vengeance) against him; so he mentioned that in order that it be known the reason for his not regarding it. ﴿"I killed a person from among them"﴾, that is, from the family of Pharaoh, ﴿"and so I fear"﴾ — that if I confront them, ﴿"that they will kill me"﴾ — for my offence against them, and for my being alone and a stranger, and for the heaviness of my tongue in establishing proofs. [Note: the "Who is Pharaoh" content is not in this passage.]

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 34:

When the request for assistance from a person who has sufficiency and for whom he has compassion followed from that, and his brother Harun was the most worthy of people of this description, the implied sense was: "So send with me my brother Harun," and so on to its end. However, he placed his mention first, out of concern for his matter, and said: ﴿And my brother Harun﴾. The apparent reading is that his waw is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject) from the pronoun of Musa, peace be upon him, or that it is conjunctive upon what was said. The meaning is that he feared the purpose of the message might be lost, either by his being killed or by his not being able to explain it. So he was content with an allusion to sufficiency (p-٢٨٤) regarding the first, because no one other than God has the power for it, and he stated explicitly what would suffice regarding the second. It is as if the implied sense was: "Indeed I fear that they will kill me, and the purpose will be lost, and nothing will protect me from that except You. And indeed my tongue has a knot in it, and my brother..." to its end. He further magnified him with the separating pronoun, and said: ﴿He is more eloquent than me in tongue﴾, meaning: in terms of speech, because of the knot that had come upon his tongue from placing the ember in his mouth when he was a child in the care of Fir'awn. ﴿So send him﴾, meaning: because of that, ﴿with me as a helper (ridʾ)﴾, meaning: an assistant, from radaʾtu fulānan bi-kadhā (I made someone a support for him with such-and-such), meaning: you made for him strength and a supporter. And radaʾtu al-ḥāʾiṭ (I propped up the wall) means when you reinforce it with wood or a beam that prevents it from falling. The recitation of Nafiʿ is without a hamza, as a derivative (ziyāda) form.

Since he had from Musa such tenderness and compassion that description falls short of it, he drew attention to that by answering the question with his words: ﴿He will confirm me﴾, meaning: by clarifying with his eloquence what I have said and explained, and establishing the proofs for it until it becomes as clear as the sun, so that he, along with his confirming me himself, will be a cause for others' confirming me. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read it in the nominative as a description of ridʾ. Then he gave the reason for this request and clarified that this is what he meant, not that he should say to him "You have spoken the truth," for his saying that word has no connection to eloquence such that it would be the cause for the request concerning it. He said, emphasizing it, because whoever is a messenger from God is not to be supposed to fear: ﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾.

(p-٢٨٥) Since what he had seen of their deeds and heard of their words made it likely that they would deny him, and since he knew the hardness and arrogance they had, he alluded to this with emphasis, meaning: "If they deny me, the argument will be hard for me, as is customary for people of resolve when opponents band together in obstinacy. Sending me entails much speech and lengthy debate." Close to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when God commanded him to warn his people: "Then they will crush my head and make it a loaf of bread." It seems that the purpose of the noble leaders, upon them be blessings, peace, greetings and honor, in asking whether the matter would follow customary course or not, was this: if it followed customary course, they would prepare themselves for death; otherwise, God would mention to them the extraordinary matter, which would be good news for them, so that they might proceed in the matter with insight and conduct themselves according to what it requires of the course of action.

When God had confirmed the request with Aaron, upon both of them be the blessings and peace, He confirmed for him the answer to the request with His words, beginning a new statement: ﴿He said: "We will strengthen your arm with your brother"﴾. He mentioned the limb most fit for bearing hardships, saying: ﴿your arm﴾, meaning your strength, ﴿with your brother﴾, meaning: We will strengthen you and support you through him, answering your request, as a kindness from you to your brother and as help from him to you. ﴿And We will grant you both authority﴾, meaning: great dominance over them and victory over them through proofs (p-٢٨٦) and awe, because of what you mentioned of fear. ﴿So they shall not reach you﴾ [i.e., so] with the result that they will not ﴿reach you﴾ with any kind of overpowering ﴿by Our signs﴾, meaning: We will make that happen because of the signs that will appear at your hands, which are attributed to Us and are magnified. Therefore the outcome was ﴿you and whoever follows you﴾, meaning from your people and others, ﴿shall be the victors﴾, meaning: not anyone else. This indicates that Pharaoh did not reach the magicians with anything of what he threatened them with, because they were among the greatest followers who gave themselves up for God. It seems that He omitted their matter here because the discussion concerns the matter of Pharaoh and his soldiers, as is evident from their repeated mention. The outcome has revealed that the magicians were not among his soldiers, but rather of the party and army of God. Nevertheless, He alluded to them with this verse and the one after it. It will come in the end of Surah al-Hadid, from the History of Ibn Abd al-Hakam, that they were saved, and some of them returned to Egypt, and they were the first to practice monasticism.

[The commentary] explained what had passed from the Torah. He said after what was previously mentioned: "And after many days the king of Egypt died, and the Children of Israel rested from the severity of their servitude. They prayed, so God heard their prayer, knew their servitude, heard their outcry, and remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. God looked upon the Children of Israel and knew their humiliation. Moses was tending the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. He drove the sheep to the edge of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. The Angel of God appeared to him in a flame of fire from within the bramble, which was burning with fire, yet the bramble was not being consumed. Moses said: 'I will turn aside and see this great sight; why is this bramble not burning?' The Lord saw that he had turned aside to look, so God called to him from within the bramble and said to him: 'Moses, Moses!' He said: 'Here I am!' He said: 'Do not come near here; take off your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is a holy place.' In another version: 'sanctified.' God said: 'I am the God of your father Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.' Moses covered his face, for he feared to lift his gaze toward the Lord. The Lord said: 'I have indeed seen the humiliation of My people in Egypt, and I have heard their outcry which they raised because of their servitude, for I know their suffering. So I have come down to deliver them from the hands of the Egyptians, and to bring them up from that land to a good, wide land flowing with milk and honey, the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites. Now the cry of the Children of Israel has come up to Me, and I have seen the oppression the Egyptians inflict on them. So now I will send you to Pharaoh, and you shall bring My people, the Children of Israel, out of Egypt.'" (p-٢٨٨) Moses said to God: "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Children of Israel out of Egypt?" God said: "I will be with you, and this will be the sign for you that I have sent you: when you bring the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain." Moses said: "Here I am, going to the Children of Israel, and I will say to them: 'The Lord, the God of your fathers, has sent me to you.' If they say to me: 'What is His name? What shall I say?' the Lord said to Moses: 'Say to them: "The Eternal One who has always been," and in another version: "who does not cease."' He said: 'Thus shall you say to the Children of Israel: "Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh" has sent me to you.'" The Lord also said to Moses: "Thus shall you say to the Children of Israel: (p-٢٨٩) 'God, the Lord of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is My name forever, and this is My remembrance to the ages of ages. Go and gather the elders of the Children of Israel and say to them: "The Lord, the God of your fathers, has appeared to me, and the God of Abraham, [Isaac] and Jacob says to you: I have remembered you and what was done to you in Egypt. I have seen your bringing out from the servitude of the people of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites—and those who preceded them—to the land flowing with milk and honey." When they accept from you, enter, you and the elders of the Children of Israel, [to] the king of Egypt, and say to him: "The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has appeared to us, so let us now go a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God." I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go, not even with a mighty hand, until I send forth My plagues and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders [that] I will work among them. After that he will send you away, [so] I will give the people favor and mercy in the eyes of the Egyptians. When you depart, you shall not go empty-handed, but each woman shall borrow from her neighbor and from the woman who lives in her house jewelry of gold and silver and clothing, and you shall put them on your sons and daughters, and you shall despoil the Egyptians." Moses answered and said: "They will not believe me, nor will they accept my word, for they will say: (p-٢٩٠) 'Why has the Lord appeared to you?'" The Lord said to him: "[What is that in your hand?" He said: "It is my staff." He said: "Throw it on the ground." He threw it on the ground and it became a serpent, and Moses fled from it. The Lord said to him]: "Moses! Stretch out your hand and take hold of its tail." [He stretched out his hand] and seized it, and it turned into a staff in his hand. He said: "So that they may believe that God, the God of their fathers, has appeared to you: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob." The Lord said to Moses: "Put your hand back into your bosom," and in another version: "into your sleeve." He put it in, then took it out, and behold, his hand was white as snow. He said to him: "Put your hand back into your bosom," and in another version: "into your sleeve." He put it back, then took it out, and behold, it was like his flesh again. "If they do not believe nor heed the first sign, they will believe and heed the other sign. If they do not believe these two signs and do not hear your word, take water from the earth," and in another version: "from the Nile," "and pour it on the ground, and it will turn and become blood on the dry land." Moses said to the Lord: "I beseech You, O Lord, I am not an eloquent man, neither since yesterday nor before that, nor since the time You spoke to Your servant, (p-٢٩١) for I am slow of speech and heavy of tongue [because I]." The Lord said to him: "Who made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, the Lord, who does that? So go now, and I will be with you, watching over your tongue and teaching you what you are to say." He said: "Moses: I beseech You, O Lord! Send by whomever else You will." He said: "This is your brother Aaron the Levite; I know that he is eloquent and fluent of speech, and he too will come to meet you, and he will rejoice greatly at seeing you." He informed him of the matter and taught him My words, and I will be watching over your mouth and his, and I will teach you both what you should do. He will speak to the people on your behalf, so he will be your interpreter, and you will be to him as a god," and in another version: "a master and a director." "Take this staff in your hand, with which you shall perform the signs." Moses returned, going to Jethro, his father-in-law, and said to him: "I am returning to my brothers in Egypt, to see whether they are still alive." Jethro said to Moses: "Go in peace and safety." The Lord said to Moses in Midian: "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead," up to what else has passed in al-A'raf. In this passage there is something that is not permissible to apply in our law to a created being, namely the title "God" (al-Ilah), which in the language of the Hebrews means "the Knower" and "the Judge." It also contains that Pharaoh died before Moses returned. If the one who raised Moses in his house, upon him be blessings and peace, is meant [by Pharaoh], then this is among what they altered.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 36:

Since the implied sense is: "He came to them as God commanded, his brother Aaron supported him as God had informed, they called them to God, and they displayed the signs they had been commanded to show," he then built on this, with the particle *fa* (indicating swiftness) showing how quickly he carried out the command: ﴿So when he came to them﴾, i.e., Pharaoh and his people.

Since Aaron's mission, peace be upon him, was only in support of Moses, peace be upon him, he indicated this by explicitly naming the one who came, saying: ﴿Moses, with Our signs﴾, i.e., those which We had commanded him to bring, which point to all the signs, because they are equal in breaking the normal course of things (*khariq al-'adah*, the breach of habitual custom, i.e., miracle). They were ﴿clear proofs﴾, i.e., in the utmost clarity. ﴿They said﴾, i.e., Pharaoh and his soldiers: ﴿This is nothing but fabricated magic﴾, [i.e., the signs] he displayed. I.e., it is an illusion with no reality, like all kinds of magic, deliberately devised to deceive, and not a *mu'jizah* (miracle, i.e., a supernatural sign) from God. ﴿We have never heard of this﴾, i.e., of the message he attributes to God, ﴿among our forefathers﴾. They pointed to the *bid'ah* (innovation) that has misled most of creation, which is making customary *taqlid* (blind imitation) the judge, especially when it has become old, over the decisive proofs, [in His saying:] ﴿of the earliest ones﴾. They lied and fabricated. Indeed, they had heard of such things in the days of Joseph, peace be upon him, as in the line of poetry: "and there is no antiquity to the covenant." The one who believed had said to them: ﴿O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ [Ghafir: 30], up to His saying: ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 34]. (p. 293)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 37:

When the Exalted One reported their statement, He followed it with the report of Moses' statement, peace be upon him, so that the listener might weigh the two speeches against each other and, by his own reason, perceive which of them is corrupt. "Things are distinguished by their opposites." This is according to the recitation of the majority (al-Jama'a), with the conjunction *wa* (and). He began a new sentence as an answer to someone who seems to have asked about his reply, according to the recitation of Ibn Kathir (qira'a, a variant reading), which omits it. The context calls for an inquiry into what he answered them when they called the manifest signs "sorcery," and so it magnifies that. He said: ﴿Moses said﴾, that is, when they denied him, and they were the liars. He pointed, for the one with insight, to a way by which they could distinguish the two matters, in a context of warning them: ﴿My Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to me in what you see of His confirming me in everything I claimed, by manifesting what you cannot accomplish with your strength of extraordinary feats, and by preventing this tyrant, the arrogant oppressor, from reaching me with harm. ﴿Knows best who has come﴾ with misguidance, in wrongdoing and transgression, so that he will be forsaken, because he is a sorcerer, then one to be burned, a fabricator against God. For him will be an evil abode. He knows his condition. But he said ﴿who has come with the guidance﴾, that is, the one whom God has permitted, and it is true in itself ﴿from Him﴾, depicting his state and stirring desire for his followers ﴿and for whom will be the good end of the abode﴾, because he is supported and aided. That is, rest, tranquility and stability, together with security, peace of mind, joy and victory in all objectives, in the state which will be the last of the states from me and from you. So he knows that he has come with what pleases God. Although its reality is whatever follows a thing of good or evil, it is not meant except what is intended for the intelligent person, so that it may belong to him. As for the evil end, it is upon him and not for him. Then he gave the reason for this by what God has made His custom, and he said, informing that the forsaken one is the liar, indicating that He is the victor because God is with him, confirming what is settled in souls, that piety is not overcome by the weak: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾, that is, they will not succeed or win. ﴿The wrongdoers﴾, that is, those who walk as one walks in darkness without a guide. They do not set a foot in a place they trust to be fit for walking, and there is no certainty in it. "You will surely see, and you will surely come to know its news after a while."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 38:

﴿And Pharaoh said﴾ as a reply to this encouragement and warning, after the admonition and the showing of the great signs, striving to repel what he saw as drawing his foolish, ignorant people away from ignorance through the manifestation of those clear signs, by holding them back from belief for some time. This was his habit whenever Musa, peace be upon him, displayed a proof, because his people were in the utmost stupidity and deep-rooted in inclining toward falsehood, averse to the truth, and preferring mere suspicion (al-maẓinna) over certain evidence (al-ma'inna): ﴿O assembly (al-mala')﴾, that is, the nobles, honouring them to win their hearts ﴿I do not know for you﴾, and he intensified the negation, saying: ﴿any god other than me﴾. He denied his knowledge of that, displaying fairness and that he did not intend to deceive them, while it is clear from him that he intended to create doubt in them, (p-295) as an indication from him that the lack of his knowledge of its existence was nothing but the absence of its existence, after his knowledge that the truth was with Musa, peace be upon him, since he exhausted what he was able to do after they saw the dazzling signs and the manifest proofs. Then he increased their holding back from following by attributing to his ignorance his saying to his vizier, instructing him in the craft of brick-making, since he was the first to make it, even though this phrasing is more like the aspirations of tyrants than saying: make bricks for me: ﴿so kindle for me﴾, he attributed the kindling to himself, informing them that it was necessary ﴿O Haman﴾, [and] he is his vizier, ﴿over the clay﴾, that is, that which is made into bricks so it becomes baked brick. Then, causally following the kindling, he said: ﴿so make for me﴾, that is, from it, ﴿a lofty structure (ṣarḥ)﴾, that is, a high building that reaches the sky. Al-Tabari said: every flat-roofed building is a ṣarḥ, like a palace. Al-Zajjaj said: every wide, elevated building. ﴿That I may ascend﴾, that is, I will strive to ascend ﴿to the god of Musa﴾, [that is,] the one he calls to, for there is no one on earth with the description he mentioned, so I seek him in the sky, giving them the impression that it is something attainable, on the assumption that the claim of his existence is correct, while he was certain of the opposite. But he intended to repel them from time to time, knowing that the custom is that most (p-296) people assume that kings have the power to do whatever they say. Then he increased their doubt by his saying, emphasizing in order to dispel what was firmly established in their souls of the truthfulness of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And indeed I think him﴾, that is, Musa, ﴿to be among the liars﴾, that is, his habit is that. He himself lied and deserved the curse of God, and he described the most truthful people of that time with the attribute long established in transgression. If this statement from him was according to its reality, then nothing is a more established testimony to the extreme of his ignorance and stupidity, in that he thought he could reach the sky. Then he reasoned, on the assumption of reaching it, that he could ascend upon it, and on that assumption he could contend with its builder, its raiser, and its elevator.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 39:

When he said this, intending by it, as has been mentioned before, to keep his people from following the truth, Allah, exalted is He, followed it with an indication that they did what he intended, [even though] that was arrogance against the truth. So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he was arrogant﴾, that is, he brought about arrogance with the utmost desire for it, ﴿he and his soldiers﴾, by his saying this, by which he barred them from the way, and by their being barred because of their intense desire for arrogance against the truth and for following falsehood, ﴿in the land﴾, that is, the land of Egypt. Perhaps He defined it (the land) as an indication that if he had been able to do that elsewhere, he would have done it. ﴿Without right﴾, that is, arrogance accompanied by the absence of this reality. The expression with the definite article (p-297) indicates that magnifying oneself with some kind of right is not arrogance, even if its form is like that. As for His arrogance, glory be to Him, it is entirely with right. He joined to this what branched off from it and from heedlessness as well, and for this reason He did not link it with fa' (then), so He said: ﴿And they thought﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his people thought with a thought upon which they built their belief in the foundation of the religion, which can only be by a decisive proof, ﴿that they to Us﴾, that is, to Our judgment specifically, in which the severing of means becomes manifest, ﴿would not be returned﴾, that is, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. Therefore they became bold in the corruption they committed.

So when their destruction had come about as a consequence of that, He said: ﴿So We seized him﴾, that is, with Our majesty, a seizing of subjugation and vengeance, ﴿and his hosts﴾, that is, all of them, and that is easy for Us. He indicated their insignificance by His saying: ﴿So We cast them into the sea﴾, that is, despite their smallness and Our greatness, ﴿into the sea﴾. Thus, despite their multitude and strength, they were like small pebbles that a mighty-armed thrower flings from his hand into the sea, so they vanished immediately, and neither they nor any of them returned to family or wealth. When this verse had given rise to knowledge that minds cannot encompass, He said: ﴿Then see﴾, that is, you who seek to know the signs and who look at them with the gaze of reflection (i'tibar, taking lessons). He increased the magnification of this by alerting that it is something worthy of being asked about, and so He said: ﴿how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, that is, what kind of existence it was, ﴿the final outcome﴾, that is, the last state of affairs of ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, however much their wrongdoing increased and their affair became hard to resolve. They went away in the blink of an eye, as if they had never existed, and they disappeared from sight as if they had never been at all, and after that command and prohibition they fell silent, becoming such that they had never been. So let those who have wronged be warned, if they persist in their wrongdoing, that they will be cut off and become as though they had never existed. This is a great indication, with the greatest good news, that the end of every wrongdoer will be like this, if the wronged one who is in the right endures patiently with him and remains steadfast until God judges, and He is the best of judges.

(p-298)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 41:

Since "Whoever establishes a good practice (sunnah hasanah), he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection, and whoever establishes an evil practice, he will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection," and since they were the first in that era to persist and to be steadfast in denying the signs and concealing the clear proofs, despite their succession and multitude, their long duration and magnitude, and since opposing the intellect and following misguidance is extremely far-fetched, especially when it guarantees destruction in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, the Exalted said, in the manner of majesty: ﴿And We made them﴾ [i.e., in this world] ﴿leaders (a'immah)﴾, meaning, those who are followed in rejecting what no intelligent person would reject of these signs. That is, We made their matter famous, so that hardly anyone would be ignorant of it. Thus, whoever does the like of their deeds, of rejecting the truth and being arrogant toward creation, it is as if he has chosen to follow [them], even if he did not intend that. So this is attributed to him, lifting him from being ascribed to doing what he is obligated to be characterized by, while he is unaware of it, just as no soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing. (p-299) And the people most worthy of being followed by them, in the inner part of their belief and the outer part of their conduct, and in the frustration of their hopes and desires, are the people of atheism through the doctrine of unity-of-existence (ittihad). May God destroy their helpers and hasten their ruin. He clarified this meaning with His saying: ﴿They call﴾, meaning, they bring about the call for whoever is deceived by their condition, so he goes astray in their misguidance, ﴿to the Fire﴾, meaning: [and We made for them helpers who support them], contrary to what We intended for the Children of Israel, as preceded at the beginning of the surah, and We made them inheritors.

Since the usual condition of leaders is victory, and He had informed about their abandonment in this world, He said: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning, which is the Day of Mutual Loss, ﴿they will not be helped﴾, meaning, they will have no kind of help at all, as they were on the day of their destruction in this world, equally; nor will they be leaders, nor will they have any call. They will abide forever in the punishment, and for them will be an evil dwelling.

When he had described this condition, he described its outcome. He said it in the position of majesty (*maẓhar al-ʿaẓama*), because the context is to show the exaltedness of Pharaoh and his people, and that despite this they are subject to God's will: ﴿And We made them follow, in this﴾. Since the intent was to elaborate (*iṭnāb*) on their dominion, he specified the demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*) and said: ﴿the world﴾. He did not say "the life," because the context is to belittle their affair and show the baseness of their station: ﴿a curse﴾, meaning expulsion and distance from Our presence [and a repelling of them by it], and a supplication against them by it from everyone who hears their story, by his tongue (p-300) if he opposes them, or by his action, which becomes for them a burden like its weight. And ﴿on the Day of Resurrection they will be﴾, meaning specifically them and those who resemble them, ﴿among the reviled﴾, meaning also those who are banished and disgraced, together with the ugliness of their faces and forms and the abomination of their words, deeds and states. It is from *qubḥ* (ugliness), which is the opposite of *ḥusn* (beauty), and from their saying "I made the thing ugly" (*qabbaḥtu al-shayʾ*), meaning I broke it, and "God made the enemy ugly" (*qabbaḥa Allāh al-ʿaduww*), meaning He removed him far from every good. How wonderful, then, is the clarity after this that Pharaoh is the enemy of God in the Hereafter just as he was His enemy in this world. So the curse of God is upon him who says that he died a believer, and that there is no explicit statement in the Qur'an that he is among the people of the Fire, and upon [every] one who doubts his disbelief after what he committed of his manifest affair.

When He, glory be to Him, had promised the leadership of the Children of Israel and related their stories, He concluded with the leadership of the household of Pharaoh, who called to the Fire. This is to inform that what they were upon must be shunned, rejected, and kept far away. It is known that every leadership needs a foundation, so the soul yearned for the basis of the leadership of the Children of Israel, which in that era must be devoted to, held fast to, and hastened toward. So He, glory be to Him, informed of that with an oath [with the opening] using the particle of expectation, because the Arabs, although they affirm the favour bestowed upon the Children of Israel by rescuing them from the hand of Pharaoh (p-301) and establishing them afterward, and by sending down the Book to them, their position of denying the establishment of the People of Islam and rejecting their Book is the position of one who denies the matter of the Children of Israel, for there is no distinction between one prophet and another, one book and another, or one people and another, since the Lord of all is One. So He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, that is, with what We possess of majesty, beauty, glory, and perfection; ﴿the Book﴾, that is, the Torah (Tawrah), which comprises guidance and good in both abodes. Abu Hayyan said: It is the first book in which obligations and rulings were revealed.

Since the ruling of the Torah does not extend to all future time, He introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿after﴾, indicating that its giving was only for a period of time, after which He, glory be to Him, abrogates it by what He wills of His command. ﴿We destroyed﴾, that is, by Our greatness, ﴿the earlier generations﴾, that is, from the people of Noah to the people of Pharaoh. He specified their time by destruction, indicating that He does not cause a nation of nations to be wholly destroyed after the revelation of its Book, honouring it and those to whom it was sent down and delivered. [Then] He mentioned its condition by saying: ﴿as insights﴾, plural of basirah, which is the light of the heart, ﴿as lamps and lights﴾ ﴿for mankind﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43], that is, they see by them what is understood of the affairs of their livelihood and their return, and their first and last states, just as by the light of the eye (p-302) one sees what is good among worldly affairs.

Since the one who seeks insight may not be guided due to some obstacle, He said: ﴿and guidance﴾ [that is,] for the one who acts by them toward every good. Since the one who is guided may sometimes be moved against someone who reached his aim while being harmful, He said: ﴿and mercy﴾, that is, a wholesome, noble blessing, because it leads to it.

Having mentioned its condition, He mentioned their condition after its revelation, saying: ﴿that they might remember﴾, that is, so that their condition would be that of one whose remembrance is hoped for. This indicates that there is nothing in the revealed laws that departs from reason; rather, whenever a person reflects upon it, he recalls from his intellect what guides to its like.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 44:

When Allah, glorified is He, had in this surah explained the wondrous aspects of the affair of Musa, peace be upon him, and his hidden circumstances, which He explained, and since these reports could not be denied by the People of the Book, a kind of denial took place. It was also well known, in the most widespread manner, that the Prophet ﷺ had not known them, nor anything else of them, apart from the One, the Subduer. Allah, glorified is He, indicated this by His saying, as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿We gave [him]﴾ [al-Qasas: 43]: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾, that is, the valley on the side of Mount Tur where Musa, peace be upon him, saw the fire, [and it is on the side of it that faces the sea, on the western side, to the right of one who turns toward the direction of the honored Makkah from the direction of Egypt], so the Mighty, the Compeller (p-303) called to him from it, and it is Tuwa. ﴿When﴾, that is, at the time when ﴿We decreed﴾ by Our speech, with what it contained of majesty, and He increased the greatness in its lofty degrees by indicating with the particle of the end-point, so He said: ﴿to Musa the command﴾, that is, the command of his being sent to Pharaoh and his people, and what We wished to do of that at its beginning and in its course [and its end] in summary. Thus everything We informed you of matches its detail to its summary. So you were not in a place where you could hear that which We decreed to him from the side on which you were. ﴿And you were not﴾, that is, in any respect ﴿among the witnesses﴾ to the details of that affair which We had summarized for Musa in that place, at its times, along with those who witnessed it from that generation, from the seventy whom he chose, or others who followed him or turned away from him, so that you could report all of it in this manner in which We have brought it to you in these miraculous styles. There is no doubt that the matter of your knowing it in this way is confined to either your witnessing it at its time, or your learning it from the Creator, or from the creatures who witnessed it, or from those who were told of it by one who witnessed it. And the absence of your having learned it from any of the creatures, in its being widely known, holds the same status as the absence of your witnessing it at its time. Therefore nothing remains except that you received it from the Creator, and that is the truth in which there is no doubt for any fair-minded person.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 45:

Since the implied sense is: "You were not among the people of that time who were present for that matter, and your life was extended to this time so that you were informed of what you had not witnessed," He corrected this by saying the opposite: ﴿But We⦆, meaning: by the greatness that belongs to Us, ﴿brought into being⦆, meaning: after We had destroyed the people of that time who knew these matters by direct observation and by report, all of them, ﴿generations⦆, meaning: We did not leave any one of the people of that time behind; rather, We destroyed them and brought into being after them many generations. ﴿Then the life span grew long for them⦆, meaning: by its passing and its extension, very much so, through the gradual course of time, little by little, so those reports were forgotten, and the monks and rabbis distorted what remained of them, especially in the era of the interval (fatrah). Therefore, in Our wisdom, it was necessary to send you, so We sent you, ﴿that you might set straight the path (mahajjah)⦆ and that the proof (hujjah) might be established through you. Thus it is known that your informing of this, while you had not witnessed it and had not learned it from any created being, is only from Us and by Our revelation.

Since He negated knowledge of this by way of witnessing, He negated the cause of knowledge of it, saying: ﴿Nor were you dwelling⦆, meaning: residing for a long period, continuously, among ﴿the people of Madyan⦆, meaning: the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, ﴿reciting⦆, meaning: reading, in the manner of narrating the traces and true reports, ﴿to them Our verses⦆, the great ones, so that you would be among those concerned with matters of revelation and would come to know the fine details of its reports. Thus their report, and the report of Musa, peace and blessings be upon him, with them, and his report after separating from them, would be part of your concerns, because your motivation at that time would be strong for learning it. ﴿But We were⦆, meaning: a pre-eternal, everlasting state of being whose attribution to all times is equal, by the greatness that belongs to Us, ﴿sending messengers⦆, meaning: We possess the attribute of power to send; so We sent to every prophet in his time, then We sent to you in this era with their reports and the reports of others, so that you might spread them among the people, clear in exposition and free from confusion, because We were witnesses to all of that; nothing of it was hidden from Us, and nothing happened except by Our command.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 46:

When he negated the originating cause of knowledge of that general account, and then the consequent cause of knowledge of the detailed events and deeds, he negated the consequent cause of knowledge of the rulings and the establishment of the Law, with its narratives, admonitions, lawful and unlawful matters, burdens and fetters, by His saying: ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when﴾, i.e., at the time when ﴿We called﴾, i.e., We caused the call to occur to Musa, peace be upon him, and We gave him the Torah and informed him of what cannot be known except from Us or from him. It is well known that you did not learn anything of that from him, because you did not associate with anyone who transmitted those reports from Musa, peace be upon him, nor did anyone transmit them from those who had transmitted them from him. Rather, that came to you from Us. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But﴾, i.e., We sent down what We intended of it and of other things upon you, revealed it to you, and sent you with it to the creatures, ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾, for you specifically and for the creation generally, ﴿that you may warn﴾, i.e., admonish (p-306) with great admonition, ﴿a people﴾, i.e., people of strength and valour, who have no obstacle to great deeds of goodness, neither turning away from you. They are the Arabs and whoever in that era of mankind ﴿had not come to them﴾, and the negation is made general by the addition of the preposition in His saying: ﴿any warner﴾, i.e., from among them. They are intended by his being sent to them. Otherwise, the messengers of Musa, peace be upon him, had come to them, then the messengers of Isa, peace be upon him. And if the report about Khalid ibn Sinan al-Absi is sound, he would be a prophet but not a messenger, or a messenger only to his own people, Bani Abs, specifically. So his calling others, if it occurred, is from the category of commanding good in general, not sending in particular. Thus the estimate is: a warner from among them in general. The addition of the preposition in His saying: ﴿before you﴾ indicates a recent time, namely the time of the interval (al-fatra, the gap between prophets). As for what preceded that, they were upon the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, until Amr ibn Luhayy altered it. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, warned them in those eras, then Isma'il, peace be upon him, then those after them among the righteous of their descendants until the time of Amr ibn Luhayy. So they, because of the absence of a warner, are blind to guidance, following the path of ruin. And He said: ﴿so that they may remember﴾, for the same reason mentioned earlier: that if they accept what you have brought and reflect upon it, I will remind them with a clear reminder, by what the manifestation (al-idhhar) has indicated, namely what is in their minds of its evidences, even though those minds would not be sufficient without it. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 47:

Since the absence of a warner coming to them before him (peace be upon him) would negate the proof against them for their punishment by what Allah has made obligatory upon Himself—and to Him belongs the conclusive proof; He is not questioned about what He does—out of His own noble self, as a bounty from Him and mercy, [Allah] mentioned that sending him was something indispensable for that, so He said: ﴿And had it not been﴾, that is: and had it not been for this which We have mentioned, We would not have sent you to warn them. But He omitted this answer out of reverence for him (ﷺ), so that it would not be confronted with it. And that which concluded the sending is ﴿that a calamity should befall them﴾, that is: at some time or other, ﴿a calamity﴾, that is: a great one, ﴿for what their hands have sent forward﴾, that is: of the sins which We have decreed are among those not pardoned, ﴿and they would say: "Our Lord﴾, that is: O You who are good to us, ﴿why did You not send to us﴾, that is: why did You not—and why would You not—﴿a messenger﴾, that is: in a manner of honor for us, so that we would be aware that we are among those whom the Most High King cares for.

He answered the specification which they likened to a command, since each of them is a motivation toward the act, by His saying: ﴿so that we would follow﴾, that is: so that the sending of Your messenger would result in our following ﴿Your signs and be﴾, that is: a state firmly established, ﴿among the believers﴾, that is: those who affirm you in everything your messenger (ﷺ) brings from you, with an eloquent affirmation. So if they said that (p-308) on the assumption that no messenger had been sent, they would have a proof in the course of your customs, even though the conclusive proof is Ours.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 48:

Since the implied sense is: "But We sent you with the truth to cut off this argument of theirs," he follows it with His saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them﴾, that is, the people of Makkah, ﴿the truth﴾, which is more general than the Book and the Sunnah and what is derived by analogy (qiyas) from them. It is in itself worthy of being accepted, being at the highest peak of firmness, so how much more so when it comes ﴿from Us﴾, with the greatness We possess, and upon your tongue, while you are the greatest of creation! ﴿They said﴾, that is, the people of the call among the Arabs and others, out of obstinacy and disbelief in it: ﴿Why was he not given﴾ signs [i.e., this one who comes with what he claims to be the truth], and it is constructed in the passive because the aim is the bare act of giving, since that is what the purpose of the message depends upon, together with the fact that the one given is known, ﴿like what was given to Moses﴾, that is, the hand and the staff and other signs which none can bring except the One Who is capable of all things.

Since bringing the like of what Moses, peace be upon him, brought would not, by their own claim, be a cause for faith [unless] it were greater than what Muhammad ﷺ brought, or unless people had not hesitated in believing in it, and since both of these conditions were absent, because the people of his time disbelieved in him, and when they asked the Jews about Muhammad ﷺ and ordered them to test him with the Spirit and the stories of the People of the Cave and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he came with what obliged them to confirm him in each of these, they refused and persisted in their disbelief, and their disbelief in him and in Moses, peace be upon them both, was part of that, it is known that the implied sense is: Did they not disbelieve in what was brought to them of clear signs, although it is like what Moses, peace be upon them both, brought, rather greater than it? ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾, that is, the Arabs and those reached by the call from the Children of Israel, or whomever God wills of them, or the sons of their kind and those who were like them in humanity and intellect in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, ﴿in what was given to Moses﴾.

Since the coming of each of them and their disbelief did not cover the entire time before, he affirmed the preposition, saying: ﴿before﴾, that is, [before] the coming of the truth through the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ to them. And since it was as if it were said: What was their disbelief in it? He said: ﴿They said﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his people and those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved, such as Qarun and those who followed him. And since it had been mentioned just before that the one who supported him was his brother, and the intended meaning was clear, he left both of them implicit and said: ﴿Two sorceries﴾, that is, he and his brother, ﴿who support one another﴾, that is, each of them helped the other in his sorcery until their sorcery became a miracle, so they overcame all the sorcerers. And the support of the sorcerers is derived from the support of the two sorceries, according to the reading of the Kufans. It is also permissible, and it is closer, that the pronoun refers to Muhammad and Moses, peace be upon them both, because it has been narrated that the Quraysh sent to the Jews and asked them about Muhammad ﷺ, and they informed them that his description is in their Book, so they said this saying. In that case the statement is a resumption answering one who seems to ask: What was their disbelief in both of them? It is said: They said, that is, the Arabs: "The two men are sorcerers," or "The two books are two sorceries, one supporting the other," while every person of understanding knows that this claim is false, because if the condition for the miraculous nature of sorcery were mutual support, the sorcery of Pharaoh would have been even more miraculous, since all the sorcerers of the lands of Egypt supported him and yet were unable to oppose what Moses, peace be upon him, displayed of the sign of the staff. As for Muhammad ﷺ, he called the people of the earth, of jinn and humankind, to oppose his Book, and informed them that they were incapable, even if some of them were supporters of others, and they failed.

Since their saying included disbelief, they stated it explicitly in their saying: ﴿And they said﴾, that is, the disbelievers of Quraysh, or the earlier ones among Pharaoh and his like: ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in each﴾ of the two sorcerers, or the two sorceries which they supported one another with, and both of them are what they brought from God, ﴿disbelievers﴾, out of audacity toward God and arrogance toward the truth.

When they said that, it was as if it had been asked, "Then what did he do?" He said: ﴿Say﴾, as a binding argument against them, "if you are truthful that I am a sorcerer and that my Book is sorcery." And likewise Moses, upon him be peace: ﴿then bring a Book﴾. By using the expression "from [ʿinda]" in describing it, rather than "from [ladun]", he indicated that he is satisfied from them with its being a wise thing that breaks the norm in its wisdom, even if it does not reach the summit of strangeness by being detached from inimitability in its composition, as with the Tawrah (Torah). So he said: ﴿from the presence of Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, who testifies that its states, wisdom and majesty come from Him. ﴿It﴾, that is, the one you have brought, ﴿is more guided than both of them﴾, that is, than what I have brought and what Moses brought. ﴿I will follow it﴾, that is, and I will leave both of them.

When he commanded them to the matter of bringing it, he mentioned its condition in the manner of condescension, to show fairness. In reality this is mockery of them. So he said: ﴿if you are﴾ [O disbelievers! with a firmly established state] ﴿truthful﴾, that is, in that we two are sorcerers. So bring what I have bound you to.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 50:

When the condition of their truthfulness was established, he clarified their falsehood on the assumption that there is no response, so he said: ﴿And if they do not respond to you﴾ [i.e., the disbelievers who demand the more guided (book) to be brought]. Since the response (istijabah) is transitive by itself to the call (du'a'), and with the preposition lam to the one who calls, and since mentioning the one who calls is more indicative of giving him attention and regard, he said [singling out the pronoun of him ﷺ, because no one else understands the comparison in guidance]: ﴿to you﴾, i.e., they should seek the response and realize it, by faith, or by bringing what you have mentioned to them and called them to, of what is more guided, from the Qur'an and the Torah, so that their truthfulness may appear. ﴿Then know﴾ you, ﴿that they only follow﴾, i.e., with the utmost of their effort, in what they are upon of disbelief and denial, ﴿their desires﴾, i.e., constantly. Most desire opposes guidance, so they are wrongdoers, not guided, indeed they are the most misguided of people. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And who is more astray﴾, i.e., among them, but He said: ﴿than one who follows﴾, i.e., with the utmost of his effort, ﴿his desire﴾, attaching the judgment to the attribute; and the qualification by His saying: ﴿without guidance﴾, i.e., clear proof and direction, ﴿from Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King who possesses all attributes of perfection. This is evidence that desire may coincide with guidance, and the expression with the reflexive form (ittiba') is evidence that the follower, even if he is a wrongdoer, may not be the greatest wrongdoer.

Since following desire in this manner is wrongdoing, he joined to it his saying, manifesting [the name] so that it would not be claimed to be restricted to them: ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King whose command none can repel, ﴿does not guide﴾, and he placed the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun for generality, so he said: ﴿the wrongdoing folk﴾, i.e., even if they are the strongest of people, because of their following their desires. So the verse is of ihtibak: he first affirmed the following of desire as evidence of its omission second, and second affirmed wrongdoing as evidence of its omission first.

(p-313) When he had gone to great lengths in these methods of bringing hidden things to light, and had greatly multiplied the setting forth of proofs for the truth and the establishment of demonstrations for the obligation to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), while they, by their turning away from all of that, were as if they denied that anything of it had come to them, He said, linking this to what is implied by its context: "We have certainly given you, in these verses, the greatest of clear proofs," alerting by the particle of expectation coupled with the particle of oath to the fact that this is something expected to be said here: ﴿And indeed We have caused the word to reach them﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, whose requirement is that the least indication from it suffices. ﴿For them﴾, that is, specifically, so that their being singled out with this is a great favor which they are obligated to thank. ﴿The word﴾, that is, We made some of the word, which in reality is no word other than it, follow some of it by sending it down in installments, some of it in the wake of other parts, so that it would be an answer to their statements and a solution to their difficulties, and so it would be closer to understanding and more fitting for reflection, together with its variety in promise and warning, news and admonitions, wisdom and counsel, rulings and benefits. We increased this to the point that its verses were miracles and its clear proofs were dazzling, like the mares of the monks on the day of the racing of rivals, in the thick of the arena, except that each of them is foremost in view.

When he had rebuked them, by this emphasis, for their exaggeration in lying, by word or by deed, in claiming that there had not come to them anything that calls for remembrance, he followed that delivery with the purpose of it, saying: ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, so that their condition would be the condition of those for whom it is hoped (p-314) that they would return to their intellects and find in what has been imprinted in them what reminds them of the truth as a reminder, by what the manifestation has pointed to.

Since remembrance includes that which pure reason alone indicates, and includes also that which is joined to reason, and since the possessor of this category is more worthy of gaining insight, it was as if it were said: "Did they remember?" It is said: "Yes, the People of the Book, who are truly its people, remembered [truly]." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾, i.e., by Our greatness with which We preserved them, ﴿the Book﴾, i.e., the knowledge from the Torah and the Gospel and other books of the prophets. They recite that as it should truly be recited, in some part of the time that was ﴿before it﴾, i.e., before the Qur'an, ﴿they﴾, i.e., exclusively, ﴿in it﴾, i.e., in the Qur'an, not in anything that contradicts it, ﴿believe﴾, i.e., they bring about faith in it at the time it reaches them, a faith that continually renews itself.

Then he emphasized this meaning with His words: ﴿And when it is recited﴾, i.e., its recitation is renewed, ﴿to them, they say﴾ hastening: ﴿We believe in it﴾. Then they gave a reason for that with their words, which indicate the utmost knowledge, emphasizing (the point) because whoever is upon a religion hardly believes that he would turn away from it, so how much more so when its origin is truth from Allah,

﴿Indeed, it is the truth﴾, i.e., the complete one, beyond which there is nothing but falsehood, together with it being ﴿from our Lord﴾, the One who is good to us. (p-315) Each of the two descriptions necessitates believing in it and affirming it. Then they gave a reason for their hastening to submission, drawing attention to the fact that they had the utmost insight into its matter, in that they recite what they have with its true recitation, not merely with their tongues. So their statement was sound, and their emphasis indicated their delight in it, which necessitates thanking Him: ﴿Indeed, we were﴾, i.e., a state that is in the utmost firmness; and he pointed out that whoever's Islam is sound, even for a short time, submits to this Book, by affirming the preposition, so He said: ﴿before it, we were Muslims﴾, i.e., submitting in the utmost submission to what came to us from Allah, whether its description or other than its description, agreed with our desires and what we were accustomed to, or opposed it. Therefore the result was inevitable.

Those (i.e., those of exalted rank) **will be given** their reward twice. He used the passive form (*yu'tawna*, "they will be given") because the focus is on the giving, and the Giver is well known. **Their reward twice** is for their faith in Him, both in the unseen and in what is witnessed, or for their faith in the first Book and then in the second Book. **For what they endured patiently** refers to their persistence in the faith that came before seeing (the Truth) after their former religion, the attachment to which (*ilf dinihimu alladhi kana*) had been pulling them away from it, along with other trials from the Sovereign, the Judge.

Since patience is not complete except through adorning oneself with good qualities and stripping oneself of bad ones, He said, conjoining it to **"they believe"** (*yu'minun*) and indicating that these actions are renewed at every moment: **And they repel evil with good**, from words and deeds, **evil**, i.e., from all of that, so they erase it by means of it.

Since part of this repelling cannot be complete except through generosity, He said: **and from what We have provided them**, i.e., by Our greatness, not by any power or strength of their own, whether little or much, **they spend**, relying in their creation on the One who provided it. Al-Baghawi said: "Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Forty men came with Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, from Abyssinia, meaning they embraced Islam. When they saw the destitution that the Muslims were suffering, they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission regarding their wealth, so they brought it and shared it with the Muslims."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 55:

When he mentioned that generosity with what souls are reluctant to give, of the surplus of wealth, is among the signs of faith, he followed it with the fact that restraint from what tongues utter of the surplus of speech is among the marks of gnosis (ʿirfān, deep knowledge of God). So He said: ﴿And when they hear idle talk﴾, meaning: that which benefits neither religion nor worldly life, such as abuse, denial, reproach and the like, ﴿they turn away from it﴾, out of nobility of character, shunning obscenity. ﴿And they say﴾, meaning: admonishing and making the one who speaks it hear (the truth): ﴿To us our deeds﴾, meaning: specifically, we will not be rewarded for any of them nor punished, ﴿and to you your deeds﴾, meaning: specifically, we will not be held accountable for any of them. So we do not busy ourselves with replying to you, because your condemnation of us does not diminish any of our reward, nor does occupying ourselves with rebutting it diminish it.

Since the meaning of this was that they were safe from them, they stated it to them explicitly, saying: (p-317) ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, meaning: from us. And since it is the custom that such a response breaks the idle talker and turns back the transgressor, they pointed out to them the ugliness of their state, as a rebuttal of their misguidance, by saying, as a justification for what preceded from their speech: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾, meaning: we do not burden ourselves to seek out ﴿the ignorant﴾, meaning: we do not want anything of their conditions, their statements, or anything else of their traits.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 28, verse 56:

Since it is well known that the soul of the Prophet ﷺ, by what it was created upon of goodness and love, desired the benefit of all the servants, especially the Arabs, because of their nearness to him ﷺ, and especially the closest of them to him in ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim), he was affected by the precedence of the People of the Book over his people. It might be that someone supposed that their non-guidance was due to a shortcoming in his supplication or in his desire for that, and that if he had desired their guidance and loved it, and had attached his lofty resolve to it, they would have been guided. This was answered by His saying, in a context of emphasis, to manifest the attribute of power, majesty and greatness: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾, meaning: [you cannot guide] his self, or his guidance by creating faith in his heart. Rather, in your hand is only the guidance which is direction (irshād) and clarification (bayān).

Since it might be supposed, on account of the reporting of the statement and its causation and similar matters, that some of their actions escape power, He said, negating this supposition and pointing out the error in its belief, with His saying: ﴿But God﴾, the One clothed in the mantle of majesty, greatness and perfection, to whom belongs all the command, ﴿guides whom He wills﴾, His guidance, (p-318) by granting success to what pleases Him. ﴿And He is best aware of those who are guided﴾, meaning: He alone is, those whom He has prepared to seek guidance from His creation for them, so that they will be rooted in it, whether they are of the People of the Book or of the Arabs, near or far.

al-Bukhari related in the Tafsir, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, may Allah be pleased with him: "He said: When Abu Talib was approaching death, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to him and found with him Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya ibn al-Mughira. He said: 'O uncle! Say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah.' Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya said: 'Do you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept presenting it to him and they kept repeating that statement, until Abu Talib's last words to them were that he was upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib, and he refused to say: There is no god but Allah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'By Allah, I will seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you.' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were of near kin﴾ [al-Tawba: 113], and Allah revealed concerning Abu Talib and said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said, from his father, may Allah be pleased with him: "It was revealed concerning Abu Talib."

In Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to [affirm] monotheism, and he said: "Were it not that the women of Quraysh would reproach me, I would have made your eye content with it." So Allah revealed the verse.

When al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) said, in wonder at the state of Quraysh, that they asked for signs like those given to Musa ﷺ (peace be upon him) and then disbelieved in him and in what was greater than that, and concluded that He knows best who is worthy of good and who is worthy of evil, this indicated turning away from grieving over anyone and turning toward general invitation to both the near and the distant alike. He said, as evidence for this, because they only follow their own desires, and it is connected by conjunction to their saying ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?﴾ [al-Qasas: 48] and ﴿They say: If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land﴾. That is, "if we follow the guidance" means to the utmost of following, ﴿the guidance﴾, that is, Islam, so that we affirm the oneness of God without associating anything with Him, ﴿with you﴾, that is, while you remain in what you are upon of opposing the people, ﴿we will be snatched﴾, that is, by any snatcher who wishes us, because we would be few among many without a helper, ﴿from our land﴾, as sparrows are snatched, because all the Arabs oppose us, and we have no comparison with their numbers or their strength, so they would hasten toward us and snatch us, that is, they would deliberately snatch us one by one, for we have no ability to sustain unity, or to prevent some of us from breaking away from others. Al-Baghawi said: "al-ikhtitaf (snatching) is seizing quickly."

Since the implied answer to this feeble speech was: "Did We not establish you, and those who followed you among them, when you had come to them with opposition like that with which they oppose the Arabs, or worse, and you have no comparison with their number or their might?", He followed it with His saying: ﴿Have We not established for them﴾, that is, in the fullest establishment, ﴿in their lands and their dwelling places by Our power﴾, ﴿a secure sanctuary﴾, that is, one of security in which every fearful one is safe, even the birds from their predators and the beasts from their hunters, to the extent that the flood-water of the outside does not enter the Sanctuary, but when it reaches it, it turns away from it. Ibn Hisham said, concerning the seizure of the Bayt by Kinanah and Khuza'ah: "Makkah in the Jahiliyyah did not tolerate injustice or aggression in it. No one transgressed in it without it expelling him." End of quotation.

A man would meet the slayer of his father or son in it and would not stir against him or harm him. Al-Azraqi related in his History of Makkah, with his chain, from Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "There were rings in the Ka'bah; a fearful person would put his hand into them and no one would trouble him. A fearful man came to put his hand in, and a man seized him and his hand became paralysed. I saw him in Islam, and he was paralysed."

It is related from Ibn Jurayj the story of the Arabs other than Quraysh, that they used to circumambulate the House naked unless Quraysh lent them clothes. A woman came and circumambulated naked, and she was beautiful. A man saw her and was taken with her, so he entered and circumambulated beside her, and he brought his upper arm close to hers, and his arm stuck to hers. The two of them went out of the mosque fleeing on their faces, terrified of the punishment that had befallen them. A shaykh of Quraysh met them and advised them to return to the place where they had committed the sin, and to supplicate and sincerely resolve never to return. They supplicated and sincerely resolved, and their arms separated, and each went off in a different direction.

With his chain, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: A man took a camel of his cousin and it was found in the Sanctuary. He said: "My camel!" The thief said: "You are lying." He said: "Then swear." So he swore by the Station (of Ibrahim). The owner of the camel stood between the Corner and the Station, spreading his hands, supplicating, and he did not leave his place supplicating until the thief's mind went and he began shouting in Makkah: "What is it to me and the camel? What is it to me and so-and-so, the owner of the camel!" This reached Abd al-Muttalib, who gathered the camel and handed it to the wronged man. He went out with it, and the other remained bewildered until he fell from a mountain, was dashed down, and the wild beasts ate him.

From Ayyub ibn Musa: a woman in the Jahiliyyah had with her a small cousin. She said to him: "My son, I am going to be away from you, and I fear that someone will wrong you. If a wrongdoer comes to you after me, then indeed Allah has a House in Makkah that nothing among the houses resembles, and it has coverings, and no corrupter approaches it. If a wrongdoer wrongs you one day, then seek refuge in it, for it has a Lord who will protect you." A man came to him, took him away, and enslaved him. He said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to bring their cattle to a sacred state (by marking them), and his master marked his back. When the boy saw the House, he recognised the description, so he got down and ran until he clung to the House. His master came to him and stretched out his hand to take him, and his hand became stiff. He stretched out the other, and it became stiff. He sought a ruling, and it was ruled that he should sacrifice a camel for each of his hands. He did so, and his hands were released; he left the boy and let him go free.

From Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad: a group of people reached Dhu Tuwa, and there was a gazelle that had come close to them. A man among them took hold of one of its legs, and his companions said to him: "Woe to you! Release it!" He began laughing and refused to release it.
